domains.name: Creative Arts & Design
domains.summary: This domain covers the literacies of fine art, design (graphic, product, fashion, interior), architecture, performance and related practice-based programmes, where much learning takes place in the studio and assessment centres on work produced, presented and explained. Language does specific jobs here: describing and interpreting visual work, presenting and defending work in critiques, writing statements and rationales that make practice legible to tutors, audiences and juries, and, at master’s and doctoral level, writing the exegesis that argues the research contribution of a practice. Schön’s (1983) account of design as a reflective conversation with materials and Kress and van Leeuwen’s (2006) visual grammar give EAP teachers ways to describe these practices, but the tacit vocabulary of a studio is local, so close collaboration with studio tutors and observation of crits is recommended.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to describe and discuss visual work, present in studio crits, and write statements, rationales and research texts that explain your practice.

stageEmphasis.foundation: On art and design foundation courses, build vocabulary for visual analysis, sketchbook annotation and confidence in presenting work in crits.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: On art and design pathways for undergraduate entry, practise describing visual work and presenting it in short simulated crits.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: On pathways for art and design master’s entrants, practise articulating an existing practice in statements and introduce writing about practice as research.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support crit participation and design rationales in studio modules, ideally with tutors present.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on articulating a practice in relation to context and theory in statements, rationales, final crits and critical reports.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Support practice-based doctoral researchers with the exegesis: method through making, contextualisation and claims of contribution.

domains.name: Business & Economics
domains.summary: This domain covers the literacies of business, management, accounting, finance and economics programmes, which together attract the largest international cohorts on UG and PGT courses. Business schools assess many simulated or live professional genres (case analyses, reports, memos, pitches, consultancy reports) oriented to decision-makers, accounting and finance assess commentary on figures and disclosures, and economics builds arguments from models, assumptions and conditional reasoning. Nathan (2013) and Zhu (2004) show that these assignment genres differ from the academic essay in purpose, structure and reader, so EAP teaching should analyse the school’s own briefs and exemplars with subject staff.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to analyse business cases, use frameworks critically, reason with economic models, comment on financial results and write the reports your business school assesses.

stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: On business pathways for undergraduate entry, contrast case analysis and the business report with the essay, and practise applying frameworks to short cases with evidence.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: On pathways for business, finance and economics master’s entrants, practise case and framework analysis, financial commentary and decision-oriented reports at the pace of a one-year degree.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embed support for case analyses, reports and economic reasoning in modules, using the school’s own briefs and exemplars.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Support the high volume of case-based, financial and consultancy genres on master’s programmes such as the MBA, MSc Management and MSc Finance, where students have little time to adjust.

domains.name: Health & Life Sciences
domains.summary: This domain covers the literacies of nursing, midwifery, medicine, allied health, pharmacy and related life-science programmes, where academic writing is tied to professional practice and patient safety. Its topics are evidence-based practice as an organising concept, writing clinical reasoning, care plans, case presentations, reflective practice writing, communication on placement and critical appraisal of research. Many of these genres are assessed against professional standards as well as academic criteria, so EAP teachers should work with clinical educators, use anonymised local exemplars and check regulator and programme requirements on confidentiality and record-keeping.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how health professionals use evidence, explain clinical reasoning, write care plans and reflections, present cases, appraise research and communicate safely with patients and colleagues.

stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: On health pathways for undergraduate entry, introduce reflective writing, evidence-based practice and the spoken patterns of patient communication before first placements.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: On pathways for health master’s entrants, many of them experienced practitioners, focus on evidence-based practice, reflective analysis and making professional reasoning explicit in academic prose.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embed support for clinical reasoning, care plans, reflective assignments and placement communication in nursing, midwifery, medicine and allied-health programmes.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Emphasise critical appraisal, clinical reasoning in complex cases and analytical reflection for practitioners taking master’s degrees.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Doctoral researchers revisit appraisal as risk-of-bias assessment; systematic review writing is covered by the research-writing topics.

domains.name: Humanities
domains.summary: This domain covers the literacies of literary studies, history, philosophy, religious studies, classics and related fields, where knowledge is built through interpretation and argument about texts, sources and ideas rather than through accumulating findings. Becher and Trowler characterise these 'soft-pure' fields as reiterative and interpretive, and Hyland (2004) shows that their writing typically has more explicit authorial presence and evaluative engagement with sources than the sciences. The topics cover close reading, working with primary sources, interpretive argument and philosophical writing, all of which reward detailed engagement with language and a sustained individual voice.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to analyse texts closely, work with primary sources, argue for an interpretation with evidence and write philosophical arguments with objections and replies.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Introduce close reading and the use of quotation as evidence on humanities foundation programmes.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: On humanities pathways for undergraduate entry, practise close analysis of short texts and the shift from summary to interpretation.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: On pathways for humanities master’s entrants, practise positioning an interpretation within critical or historiographical debate.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support close reading and interpretive essays in subject modules, using the department’s exemplars.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Emphasise original interpretation, engagement with critical debates and archival or primary-source work for dissertations.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Support doctoral researchers in sustaining interpretive arguments across chapters and in archival research and citation.

domains.name: Law
domains.summary: This domain covers the literacies of studying law in English, with a primary focus on common-law systems such as England and Wales: the register and terms of art of legal English, reading and briefing cases, reading legislation, answering problem questions, writing legal essays, arguing orally in moots and writing law dissertations. Legal knowledge is constructed through authoritative texts (judgments and statutes) whose language is itself the object of analysis, so reading precision and the handling of authority are central (Bhatia, 1993; Twining & Miers, 2010), and doctrinal research has its own method (Hutchinson & Duncan, 2012). Many international law students, especially on LLM programmes, trained in civil-law or mixed systems, which makes it particularly important to make common-law conventions explicit.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to read cases and legislation, use legal terms precisely, answer problem questions, write legal essays and dissertations, and argue orally in moots.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Introduce legal vocabulary and the idea of precedent in law foundation programmes.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: On law pathways for LLB entry, practise reading short judgments and statutes and contrast problem questions with essays.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: On pathways for LLM entrants, many trained in civil-law systems, make reasoning from precedent explicit and introduce legal essays, OSCOLA and dissertation method.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embed support for case briefing and problem questions in first-year LLB modules, where the conventions are new to everyone, and for mooting later.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Support LLM students in reading common-law materials efficiently and writing analytical legal essays and dissertations with OSCOLA referencing.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Support doctoral law researchers in stating their method and sustaining doctrinal or socio-legal argument across a thesis.

domains.name: Science, Engineering & Computing
domains.summary: This domain covers the discourse of the natural sciences, engineering, mathematics and computing: how technicality, grammatical metaphor and taxonomies build scientific knowledge, and how learners produce explanations, protocols and specifications, experimental language, research records, proofs and software documentation. These fields are typically hard disciplines in Becher and Trowler’s terms, with cumulative knowledge, high consensus on method and texts in which visuals, notation and code carry much of the meaning. Teaching works best when EAP staff analyse departmental exemplars with subject lecturers, because conventions differ between, for example, a chemistry protocol, a civil engineering specification and a computing README.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how scientists, engineers, mathematicians and programmers use English to explain, specify, prove, document and keep research records, and how to write these texts as your department expects.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build control of scientific explanation and the language of science and experimentation alongside subject content, using textbook and practical-class texts.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: On science and engineering pathways for undergraduate entry, raise awareness of technicality and nominalisation and practise scientific explanation and experimental language.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: On pathways for science, engineering and computing master’s entrants, focus on reading dense research prose and on precise experimental language.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embed work on experimental language, specifications, proofs and documentation in modules, ideally co-designed with subject staff around real assignments.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on research-project records, precision in specifications and design documentation, and the conventions of the student’s specialism.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Support research records and data management, protocol and methods writing, documentation of research software and the conventions of mathematical and technical publication.

domains.name: Social Sciences & Education
domains.summary: This domain covers the literacies of sociology, politics, social policy, international relations, psychology, education and related fields. Key concepts are often contested, several research paradigms coexist and writers are expected to justify their conceptual and methodological choices explicitly, while psychology combines this with the tightly conventionalised experimental report and education with practice genres such as lesson-plan rationales and teaching reflections. The topics address working with contested concepts, justifying methodology, the process texts of qualitative research, policy analysis, psychology reports and education practice genres, which recur from UG coursework to doctoral theses. Because expectations vary between fields and between supervisors, analysis of local exemplars with subject staff is essential.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to define contested concepts, justify your methods, keep qualitative field notes, write psychology reports and teaching documents, and analyse policy.

stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: On social science pathways for undergraduate entry, introduce contested concepts and the idea that definitions must be justified.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: On pathways for social science, psychology and education master’s entrants, introduce contested concepts and the expectation that methods are justified, and practise the rationale and reflective genres of teacher education.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support concept work, psychology reports, policy analysis and the methods of final-year projects.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on methodology chapters, qualitative analysis, policy analysis and TESOL and education practice genres in master’s programmes, where many students are new to the paradigms of the field.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Support doctoral researchers in articulating paradigms, operationalising concepts and accounting for extended qualitative analysis.

topics.name: Studio critiques
topics.description: Take part in studio critiques (crits) in their various forms, from one-to-one desk crits to group crits and formal reviews with a panel: present work concisely by explaining intentions, process and key decisions; listen to and clarify critique; respond to challenges by explaining or reconsidering choices without defensiveness; and give peers specific, constructive critique. Crits are a central, often assessed, speech event in art and design education with conventions and a vocabulary that are rarely made explicit.
masteryEvidence: Introduces their work in two to three minutes, covering intention, process and the main decisions, rather than describing every stage
Asks clarifying questions when critique uses unfamiliar or figurative studio language
Responds to a critical comment by explaining the reasoning behind a decision or by acknowledging and exploring an alternative
Gives a peer critique that describes what they see, interprets it and suggests a specific development
Records the main points of critique and identifies actions for the next iteration
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to present a piece of their own work (or an image provided) for two minutes, then put two challenging questions to them, one using vague studio language ('It doesn't quite resolve'). Check whether they explain intention and decisions, ask what the vague comment means, and respond to the challenge by reasoning rather than either apologising or rejecting it.

topics.name: Artist and design statements
topics.description: Write short statements, typically 50 to 300 words, that explain the concept, materials and process, and context of a work or body of practice for a specific purpose such as an exhibition label, degree show, portfolio or application. Effective statements are concrete and specific, usually written in the present tense, in the first person for statements the artist or designer authors but often in the third person for wall labels, catalogue entries and short bios, and connect the work to influences or ideas without inflated or unexplained theoretical language.
masteryEvidence: States what the work is and what it explores in the opening sentence
Describes materials and processes concretely enough for a reader to picture the work
Connects the work to a relevant context (artists, designers, ideas or issues) and explains the connection
Adapts length, register and emphasis to the purpose and audience (exhibition visitor, admissions panel, client)
Replaces vague or inflated expressions with specific claims about the work
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 150-word statement full of abstract claims ('This work interrogates the liminal space of contemporary identity') with no concrete description. Ask them to revise it for a degree-show visitor. Check whether the revision names the work and medium, describes something visible, explains the idea in plain terms and keeps one specific contextual reference.

topics.name: Design rationale and process documentation
topics.description: Document and justify the design process in sketchbooks, process journals, annotated boards and written rationales: record research, ideation, development, testing and refinement; explain each significant decision with reference to the brief, users, constraints and precedents; show alternatives considered and why they were rejected; and evaluate the outcome against the brief. Rationales make the designer's reasoning visible to assessors and are a major component of many practice-based assessments.
masteryEvidence: Annotates process images with brief notes that explain why a change was made, not only what was done
Links key design decisions explicitly to the brief, user needs, constraints or precedents
Presents at least one rejected alternative and the reasons for rejecting it
Evaluates the final outcome against the brief's criteria, acknowledging what did not work
Integrates images and text so that each annotation refers clearly to a specific visual
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three development images from a design project (their own or provided) and ask them to write an annotation of no more than 40 words for each and a 100-word rationale for the final choice. Check whether annotations explain reasons, refer to specific visible features and connect to a brief or user need, and whether the rationale mentions an alternative and a limitation.

topics.name: Visual analysis
topics.description: Describe, analyse and interpret visual works such as artworks, designs, photographs, buildings and adverts using disciplinary vocabulary: formal elements (composition, line, colour, tone, texture, scale, space, medium), and social semiotic concepts such as salience, framing, information value and gaze. Move from what is visible to what it means in context, distinguishing observation from inference and hedging interpretations appropriately. Visual analysis underpins crits, statements, contextual studies essays and design rationales.
masteryEvidence: Describes a work's composition systematically using spatial language and formal vocabulary
Distinguishes observable features from interpretations and marks inferences with appropriate hedging
Explains how specific formal choices (for example placement, salience, framing, colour) contribute to meaning
Relates the work to its context of production and reception when interpreting it
Uses disciplinary terminology accurately and explains it where the reader may not know it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner an image they have not seen before and ask for a 150-word analysis. Check whether they begin with systematic description, use formal or social semiotic vocabulary accurately, link at least two formal features to an interpretation, hedge interpretive claims and avoid stating personal preference as analysis.

topics.name: Business case analysis
topics.description: Write a business case analysis or case report: identify the central problem in an organisational case, analyse its causes with appropriate frameworks and the data in the case, generate and evaluate options against explicit criteria, and make justified, feasible recommendations for a named decision-maker. The genre is problem- and decision-oriented rather than thesis-led and is among the most common assessments in business schools.
masteryEvidence: States the central problem of the case in one or two sentences and distinguishes it from its symptoms
Uses case data and exhibits as evidence for each analytic point, with explicit interpretation
Generates at least two realistic options and evaluates each against stated criteria such as cost, feasibility, risk and fit with strategy
Makes recommendations that follow from the analysis and include implementation considerations
States assumptions where the case information is incomplete
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a one-page mini-case and 20 minutes. Ask for a problem statement, two options and a recommendation in note form. Check whether the problem is a cause rather than a symptom, whether options are evaluated against criteria and whether the recommendation follows from the evaluation rather than from general opinion.

topics.name: Language of economic reasoning
topics.description: Control the language economists use to reason with models: stating assumptions, holding other factors constant (ceteris paribus), conditional and counterfactual predictions, comparative statics (what happens to equilibrium when one variable changes), marginal reasoning, and the distinction between positive and normative statements. It also includes describing diagrams precisely (a shift of a curve versus a movement along it) and distinguishing causal from correlational claims in empirical economics.
masteryEvidence: States the assumptions of a model before using it to predict an outcome
Uses ceteris paribus and conditional structures accurately to express what a model predicts when one variable changes
Distinguishes a shift of a curve from a movement along it in describing a diagram
Separates positive (descriptive or predictive) from normative (evaluative) statements in their own writing
Qualifies empirical claims to reflect whether the evidence is causal or correlational
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner a supply-and-demand diagram in which a tax shifts the supply curve. Ask them to explain in writing what happens to price and quantity and why. Check for explicit assumptions or ceteris paribus, correct use of shift versus movement along, conditional or causal sequencing, and avoidance of normative judgement unless asked.

topics.name: Professional business genres
topics.description: Write and present the simulated professional genres business schools assess: memos, briefing notes, management reports and pitches. These genres put the main point or recommendation first, are organised for a busy decision-maker, use informative headings and selective bullet points, and adjust tone and directness to the relationship between writer and reader. Their conventions differ from the academic essay and can vary between schools and industries.
masteryEvidence: Places the purpose and main recommendation at the start of a memo or briefing note
Uses informative headings and bullet points where they help a reader act, and continuous prose where reasoning is needed
Adjusts directness and politeness to the reader's role and the relationship implied in the brief
Delivers a pitch that moves from problem to proposed solution, benefits, evidence and a clear request
Writes to the length and format conventions given in the brief or a company template
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 400-word essay-style answer to a business question and ask them to rewrite it as a 150-word memo to a named manager. Check whether the recommendation moves to the opening, headings or structure reflect the reader's decision, and tone suits the relationship.

topics.name: Applying management frameworks critically
topics.description: Use management frameworks such as SWOT, PESTLE, Porter's Five Forces and the value chain as analytical tools: choose a framework that fits the question, support each entry with case evidence, prioritise factors by significance, draw out implications for the organisation, and acknowledge the framework's limitations. Markers commonly criticise frameworks presented as unprioritised lists without analysis or implications.
masteryEvidence: Justifies the choice of framework in relation to the question being asked
Supports each factor with specific evidence from the case or external data
Ranks or weights factors and explains why the most significant ones matter
States the implication of each key factor for the organisation's decision
Identifies at least one limitation of the framework for the case in hand
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a student SWOT table with eight unsupported bullet points and ask them to turn it into one analytical paragraph. Check whether they select and prioritise rather than list, support claims with evidence, link internal factors to external ones and state implications.

topics.name: Evidence-based practice
topics.description: Understand evidence-based practice as the integration of the best available research evidence with clinical expertise and the values and circumstances of the patient, not as following research alone. In academic work this means framing focused clinical questions with a framework suited to the question (for example PICO for intervention questions, or PEO or SPIDER for questions about experience), recognising evidence hierarchies and their limits, and writing assignments in which recommendations for practice are justified by appraised evidence, professional judgement and patient perspective.
masteryEvidence: Explains the components of evidence-based practice and why research evidence alone does not determine a care decision

Turns a clinical scenario into a focused, searchable question using a framework suited to the question type (for example PICO for an intervention question, PEO or SPIDER for a question about patient experience)
Places study designs in a conventional hierarchy of evidence and explains at least one limitation of hierarchies (for example for questions about patient experience)
Justifies a recommendation in an assignment by linking it to appraised evidence, practice context and patient preference
Distinguishes evidence-based statements from tradition- or authority-based ones in a clinical text
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short clinical scenario in which the best-supported intervention conflicts with the patient's stated preference. Ask them to write a paragraph recommending a course of action. Check whether they cite the evidence and its strength, acknowledge the patient's values and professional judgement, and avoid presenting the research finding as automatically decisive.

topics.name: Reflective practice writing in health
topics.description: Write structured reflections on placement or practice experiences using a model the programme specifies (for example Gibbs's reflective cycle or a What? So what? Now what? model), moving from a concise, anonymised account of an event to analysis that draws on literature and professional standards, and ending with a concrete plan for future practice. Reflective writing is assessed throughout health programmes and in professional revalidation, and is judged on depth of analysis and professional judgement, not on confession.
masteryEvidence: Keeps the descriptive stage brief and anonymises people and settings in line with professional confidentiality requirements
Moves between past tense for the event, present tense for analysis and theory, and future or modal forms for the action plan
Explains why something happened by linking the experience to research, theory or professional standards, not only to personal feelings
Acknowledges own contribution and limitations in a professional, measured register
Produces an action plan with specific, achievable changes linked to the analysis
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 300-word student reflection that is two-thirds description and ends with 'I learned a lot and will do better next time'. Ask them to identify what the marker would criticise and to rewrite the ending. Check whether they spot the imbalance between description and analysis, the absence of literature, and the vague action plan, and whether their rewrite proposes a specific change linked to an identified cause.

topics.name: Case presentations
topics.description: Deliver and write case presentations in which patient information is selected and ordered conventionally (presenting complaint, history, examination, investigations, assessment and plan) to support clinical decision-making for a particular audience, such as a ward round, a handover or a teaching session. Effective presentations select for relevance rather than completeness, distinguish findings from interpretation, use only approved abbreviations and respect confidentiality. They differ from published clinical case reports, which follow their own reporting guidance, and from care plans (dhl.care-plans).
masteryEvidence: Presents a case in the conventional order used by the programme, selecting information relevant to the clinical problem rather than recounting everything
Adjusts length and detail to the setting, for example a brief ward-round presentation or a fuller teaching presentation
Distinguishes subjective information from objective findings, and findings from interpretation
Ends with an assessment and plan that follow from the information presented
Uses only locally approved abbreviations, expands any that could be misread and anonymises patient details
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a disordered set of notes about a fictional patient and ask for a two-minute case presentation for a ward round. Check whether they follow the expected order, foreground information relevant to the presenting problem, separate findings from interpretation, and end with an assessment and plan that follow from what was presented.

topics.name: Professional communication in health placements
topics.description: Communicate safely and appropriately with patients, families and colleagues on placement: structuring consultations, asking open and closed questions, explaining in lay terms and checking understanding, responding to emotion, seeking consent, and giving concise structured handovers or escalations to colleagues. On placement, language is part of clinical safety and is assessed against professional standards; it also involves understanding colloquial and regional ways patients describe symptoms.
masteryEvidence: Explains a procedure or condition to a lay person without unexplained jargon and checks understanding by asking the person to say it back in their own words
Uses open questions to elicit a patient's account and closed questions to clarify specific details
Acknowledges a patient's concern or emotion before giving information
Gives a concise structured handover or escalation in the format used on the placement
Recognises common colloquial descriptions of symptoms and clarifies them rather than guessing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Role-play a three-minute exchange in which the learner explains a simple procedure (for example taking a blood pressure reading) to an anxious patient who uses a colloquial expression. Check for lay terminology, an acknowledgement of the concern, a clarification question about the expression and a check of understanding that asks the patient to explain back rather than 'Do you understand?'.

topics.name: Critical appraisal of health research
topics.description: Appraise a single health research study with a structured tool suited to its design (for example a CASP or JBI checklist) and write up the appraisal as a reasoned judgement about its validity, results and applicability to a practice question. Appraisal assignments are common in health programmes and are marked on judgement, not on checklist completion. Writing systematic and scoping reviews, which builds on appraisal, is covered by res.systematic-review-writing.
masteryEvidence: Selects an appraisal tool appropriate to the study design and justifies the choice
Turns checklist answers into continuous prose that weighs strengths and weaknesses and reaches an overall judgement about trustworthiness and applicability
Explains how each major weakness is likely to affect the results, distinguishing serious threats to validity from minor limitations
Uses appraisal vocabulary accurately (risk of bias, confounding, generalisability, attrition, blinding)
Calibrates conclusions about applying the findings to the quality of the study and to the practice context
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the abstract and methods summary of a small randomised trial with one clear weakness (for example high attrition without intention-to-treat analysis). Ask for a 150-word appraisal paragraph. Check whether they identify the weakness, explain its likely effect on the result, balance it against strengths and reach a calibrated conclusion about applying the findings.

topics.name: Close reading and textual analysis
topics.description: Analyse how a passage creates meaning through its language and form, noticing patterns of word choice, imagery, syntax, sound, structure, point of view and genre, and moving from observation to interpretation by explaining what each feature does and why it matters. Close reading underpins literary studies and is also used in history, philosophy and cultural studies; a multilingual reader's sensitivity to language is a resource for it.
masteryEvidence: Identifies patterns (repetition, contrast, shifts in tense or voice) in a short passage, not only isolated features
Names features with appropriate critical terminology (for example metaphor, enjambment, free indirect discourse) and explains their effect
Moves from what the text says to how and why it says it, in a chain of observation, analysis and interpretation
Supports interpretations with brief, precisely chosen quotations analysed at word level
Considers more than one plausible reading of an ambiguous detail
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner an eight-to-twelve-line passage (poem or prose) and 15 minutes to write one analytical paragraph. Check whether they identify a pattern rather than list devices, quote briefly and analyse specific words, explain effects in relation to meaning and avoid paraphrasing the content.

topics.name: Working with primary sources
topics.description: Interpret primary sources such as documents, letters, images, objects and archival records by sourcing them (who produced them, when, why and for whom), contextualising them in their period, corroborating them against other sources, reading them closely and noting their silences. Write about them with appropriate caution and cite them in the conventions of the discipline, including archival locations and translations. Whether a source counts as primary depends on the research question.
masteryEvidence: Identifies author, date, intended audience and purpose of a source and explains how they affect its reliability for a given question
Places a source in its historical or cultural context and avoids anachronistic judgement
Corroborates a claim by comparing at least two sources and accounts for discrepancies
Explains why the same text can be a primary source for one question and a secondary source for another
Cites archival and primary materials in the department's required style, including repository details and translation information
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short primary document (for example a nineteenth-century newspaper report) and ask for a 150-word commentary on what it can and cannot tell a historian about the event. Check for sourcing (author, purpose, audience), contextualisation, at least one limitation tied to the source's nature and avoidance of reading it as a neutral record.

topics.name: Interpretive argument
topics.description: Write essays that argue for an interpretation of texts, sources or events: pose an arguable interpretive thesis, build it through analysed textual or documentary evidence, position it in relation to existing critical or historiographical readings, address alternative readings and sustain an evaluative voice. Disciplinary conventions differ, for example the present tense for discussing literary works and the movement in history from recounting events to explaining and arguing about them.
masteryEvidence: States an interpretive thesis that a reasonable reader could dispute, rather than a summary or a fact
Builds each paragraph around an interpretive claim supported by analysed quotation or source evidence
Positions the argument in relation to named critics or historians, agreeing, extending or challenging them
Addresses a plausible alternative reading and explains why their interpretation is more persuasive
Uses the tense conventions of the discipline (for example the literary present) consistently
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three candidate thesis statements on a set text or historical question (one summary, one fact, one interpretive claim) and ask them to choose the strongest and write the first body paragraph. Check whether they choose the interpretive claim and whether the paragraph opens with a claim, uses short quotation evidence with analysis and links back to the thesis.

topics.name: Philosophical writing
topics.description: Write philosophy essays that reconstruct an argument charitably in premise–conclusion form, evaluate whether it is valid and whether its premises are true, raise objections (including counterexamples and thought experiments), consider replies, and defend a position with clear distinctions and definitions. Philosophical prose values clarity, precision and explicit signposting over rhetorical flourish, and commonly uses the first person to mark the writer's argumentative moves.
masteryEvidence: Reconstructs a philosopher's argument as numbered premises and a conclusion in their own words, faithfully and charitably
Distinguishes validity from soundness and identifies which premise an objection targets
Develops an objection with a counterexample or thought experiment and anticipates the strongest reply
Draws explicit distinctions between senses of a key term when the argument depends on them
Signposts argumentative moves in the first person (I will argue, I now consider an objection) with appropriate density
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short paragraph from a philosophical text presenting an argument. Ask them to set it out as numbered premises and a conclusion and then write one objection to a named premise. Check for a faithful, charitable reconstruction, a valid structure, an objection aimed at a specific premise and use of a counterexample or reason rather than mere disagreement.

topics.name: Legal language and register
topics.description: Recognise the distinctive features of legal English and why they exist: terms of art with fixed legal meanings (consideration, negligence, estoppel), everyday words with specialised legal senses (party, action, hold, find), Latin and Law French expressions, binomials such as null and void, deontic modals, long sentences with embedded qualifications, and the plain-language movement's critique of archaic drafting. Legal terms are tied to a particular legal system, so their meaning cannot be assumed from another jurisdiction or from a bilingual dictionary.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes the legal from the everyday sense of sub-technical words such as consideration, action, hold and party in context
Uses common terms of art and Latin expressions (ratio decidendi, obiter dicta, mens rea) accurately in their own writing
Explains the function of features such as qualifications inserted within sentences in legislative drafting
Identifies where a legal concept in English law has no exact equivalent in another legal system they know and avoids false equivalence
Chooses plain, precise wording in their own analysis instead of imitating archaic drafting forms
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner five sentences from law reports, each containing a word used in its legal sense (for example 'The court held…', 'there was no consideration'). Ask them to explain each word's meaning in context. Check whether they give the legal rather than everyday sense and whether they can say why the everyday sense would mislead.

topics.name: Reading and briefing cases
topics.description: Read law reports strategically and brief them: use the citation, court and headnote to orient (knowing that the headnote is an editor's summary, not authority), then identify the material facts, procedural history, legal issues, the parties' arguments, the decision, the ratio decidendi and any obiter dicta, and note concurring or dissenting judgments. Case reading is the foundation of common-law study because legal rules are extracted from, and argued about through, judgments.
masteryEvidence: Produces a case brief with facts, procedural history, issues, decision, reasoning, ratio and notable obiter dicta under conventional headings
Distinguishes material from non-material facts and explains why the distinction matters for the ratio
Separates the ratio from obiter statements and explains why they have different precedential weight
Identifies which judges agreed, concurred for different reasons or dissented, and what that means for the case's authority
Uses the court hierarchy to explain whether a case binds or only persuades a later court
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short appellate judgment extract (about 600 words) with one obiter remark. Ask for a five-line case brief. Check whether they separate material facts from background, state the legal issue as a question, give the decision, formulate the ratio at an appropriate level of generality and identify the obiter remark as such.

topics.name: Legal problem questions
topics.description: Answer hypothetical fact scenarios by advising a party: identify every legal issue the facts raise, state the relevant rule with authority, apply it to the specific facts (including by analogy with and distinction from decided cases), consider alternative interpretations where facts are uncertain, and reach a reasoned, appropriately hedged conclusion. IRAC (Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion) and variants such as CLEO are widely taught scaffolds, but lecturers differ on them and critics note that applied mechanically they encourage rule-stating without application.
masteryEvidence: Identifies all the legal issues in a scenario, including less obvious ones, and orders them logically
States each rule concisely with supporting authority from cases or statute
Spends most of the answer applying rules to specific facts, analogising with and distinguishing precedents
Deals with missing or ambiguous facts by stating alternatives (if…; if, however,…) rather than inventing facts
Concludes with advice whose certainty reflects the strength of the analysis (likely, arguable, unlikely)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short problem scenario raising two issues and 25 minutes to answer one. Check whether they find both issues, state the rule with an authority, apply it to the particular facts rather than reciting the law, handle an ambiguous fact explicitly and give a hedged conclusion addressed to the party they are advising.

topics.name: Reading legislation
topics.description: Navigate and interpret legislation: use its structure (long and short title, parts, sections, subsections, paragraphs, schedules, interpretation and commencement provisions) to find relevant provisions, follow cross-references and definitions (including the difference between 'means' and 'includes'), parse qualifications such as subject to, notwithstanding and unless, and recognise both the traditional textbook approaches to interpretation (literal, golden and mischief rules) and the contextual, purposive approach that UK courts now describe as the modern method. Statutory text is drafted for precision and comprehensiveness, so reading it requires slow, structural parsing.
masteryEvidence: Locates a provision using its section and subsection numbering and cites it accurately
Breaks a long statutory sentence into its main rule, conditions, exceptions and qualifications
Follows defined terms to the interpretation section and explains how the definition affects the provision
Explains how a provision introduced by 'subject to' or 'notwithstanding' relates to another provision
Identifies an ambiguity in a provision and outlines how different interpretive approaches might resolve it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a statutory subsection of 60–100 words containing a condition and an exception. Ask them to rewrite it as a short flowchart or a numbered list of conditions. Check whether the main rule, conditions and exception are correctly identified and whether 'and' and 'or' between conditions are read correctly.

topics.name: Legal essays
topics.description: Write essays that argue a position about the law or legal policy: explain the current law accurately from primary authority, analyse its coherence and development, evaluate it from doctrinal, theoretical, socio-legal or law-reform perspectives using academic commentary and official reports, and sustain a thesis in answer to the question. Legal essays rely on a hierarchy of authority, use reporting verbs with legal meanings (a court holds, a judge observes, counsel submits) and are usually referenced with footnotes in OSCOLA.
masteryEvidence: States a thesis that answers the question and sustains it across the essay
Distinguishes primary authority (cases, legislation) from secondary commentary and weights them accordingly
Uses reporting verbs accurately for courts, judges, counsel and commentators (held, observed, submitted, argued)
Evaluates the law against explicit criteria such as certainty, fairness, coherence or policy aims rather than only describing it
References authorities in OSCOLA footnotes with correct neutral or report citations and pinpoints
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 'Critically evaluate…' question and a paragraph from a student essay that summarises three cases in turn. Ask them to rewrite it to serve an argument. Check whether the rewrite subordinates case description to a claim, uses 'held' only for the court's decision, evaluates against a stated criterion and adds OSCOLA footnotes.

topics.name: The language of science
topics.description: Recognise how scientific English builds knowledge through technical terms organised into taxonomies, chains of interlocking definitions, grammatical metaphor (especially nominalisation) and high lexical density, and explain what each does for the scientific reader. Understanding these features as functional, not as obscurity, lets learners unpack dense textbook and research prose and begin to produce it.
masteryEvidence: Unpacks a nominalised scientific sentence into a sequence of congruent clauses (who did what, what caused what) and repacks it
Identifies the taxonomic relations (type-of, part-of) among technical terms in a textbook section and represents them as a diagram
Distinguishes a technical term from an everyday word with the same form (work, force, power, stress, solution) and uses each in the right register
Explains how a nominal group such as a process noun lets a writer treat a previous event as the starting point of the next clause
Judges when a nominalisation in their own writing aids flow and when it hides the agent or the causal relation the reader needs
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a two-sentence extract from a first-year science textbook containing at least two nominalisations and one technical term defined earlier in the chapter. Ask them to rewrite it as it might be explained aloud to a classmate, then name which words are technical. Check that they recover the processes and participants hidden in the nominalisations without changing the causal relation and that they keep the technical term rather than replacing it with a loose synonym.

topics.name: Scientific explanations
topics.description: Write and present explanations of how or why phenomena occur, choosing among sequential explanations (a chain of events in time), causal and factorial explanations (multiple causes), consequential explanations (multiple effects) and theoretical explanations that apply a model or law to a case. Explanation is one of the most frequently assessed genres in undergraduate science and engineering and underlies exam answers, lab-report discussions and textbook learning.
masteryEvidence: Selects an explanation type that fits the question (for example a sequential explanation for a cycle, a factorial explanation for a multi-cause outcome)
Opens with an identifying statement of the phenomenon and then stages the explanation in a logically ordered series of steps or factors
Makes causal links explicit with verbs, conjunctions and nominalised causes rather than relying on 'and then'
Integrates a labelled diagram or equation and refers to it at the relevant step
Applies a named model or law to a specific case and states where the model's assumptions limit the explanation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to explain in about 150 words why a metal spoon in hot water feels hotter than a wooden one, or a comparable phenomenon from their subject. Check whether they identify the phenomenon first, order the causal steps, make each causal link explicit, use the relevant technical terms (for example thermal conductivity) correctly and avoid narrating a single experiment instead of explaining the general mechanism.

topics.name: Protocols and specifications
topics.description: Read and write procedural and specification texts used in laboratories and engineering: experimental protocols and standard operating procedures, method statements, and requirements or design specifications. This involves numbered imperative steps with exact quantities, conditions and tolerances, safety notes placed before the hazardous step, and requirement statements that use modal verbs consistently (often shall or must for mandatory, should for recommended, may for optional) so that each statement can be verified.
masteryEvidence: Writes a protocol whose steps another student can follow without asking questions, with quantities, units, conditions and timings stated
Places cautions and warnings before the step they apply to and separates them visually from the instruction
Distinguishes the imperative mood of a protocol from the past passive of a lab-report method and converts between them
Writes requirement statements that are single, unambiguous and testable, and uses modal verbs consistently with the convention the department or standard specifies
Identifies ambiguity in a specification (vague quantifiers, undefined terms, compound requirements) and rewrites it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three faulty requirement statements, for example one that bundles two requirements, one with a vague quantity ('fast', 'approximately') and one that mixes should and must. Ask them to rewrite each so that a tester could pass or fail it. Check for one requirement per statement, measurable criteria with units, and consistent modal use.

topics.name: Language of experimentation
topics.description: Use the language of experimental design and measurement precisely: testable hypotheses and predictions, independent, dependent and controlled variables, control conditions, random and systematic error, accuracy versus precision, and statements of uncertainty (for example with ± and appropriate significant figures). Many of these words have everyday meanings (error, control, significant, precise) that differ from their technical sense, so misuse signals misunderstanding of method as well as of language.
masteryEvidence: Writes a hypothesis and a corresponding prediction that state the expected relationship between named independent and dependent variables
Identifies the controlled variables and the control condition in a described experiment and explains why each is needed
Distinguishes random from systematic error and accuracy from precision, and proposes an appropriate improvement for each
Reports a measured value with its uncertainty and a number of significant figures consistent with that uncertainty
Uses 'significant' only in its statistical sense in results writing, and chooses other wording for importance
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short description of a simple experiment with one flaw (for example a thermometer that reads 2 °C high throughout). Ask them to name the variables, state the hypothesis, identify the type of error and say whether it affects accuracy or precision. Check that they classify the flaw as systematic error affecting accuracy, not precision, and that they use the variable terms correctly.

topics.name: Software and technical documentation
topics.description: Write the main documentation genres of computing for their distinct readers: README files that tell a newcomer what a project does and how to install, run and contribute to it; code comments and docstrings that explain intent and non-obvious decisions rather than restating the code; API reference entries that specify parameters, return values, errors and examples; and design documents that set out context, goals and non-goals, alternatives considered and trade-offs. Documentation is assessed in computing projects and is a core professional literacy.
masteryEvidence: Produces a README that a peer can use to install and run the project, with a one-sentence purpose statement, prerequisites, usage example and licence or contribution note
Writes comments that explain why code does something or warn of a non-obvious constraint, and removes comments that merely paraphrase the code
Documents a function or endpoint with parameter types, return values, error conditions and a minimal working example in a consistent format
Writes a design-document section that compares at least two alternatives against stated criteria and justifies the choice
Adjusts terminology and assumed knowledge for end users, contributors and maintainers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 15-line function with no documentation and two existing comments, one useful and one that restates the code. Ask them to write a docstring and decide which comment to keep. Check that the docstring states purpose, parameters, return value and at least one error case, and that they keep the comment explaining intent and delete the redundant one.

topics.name: Mathematical writing and proofs
topics.description: Write proofs and worked solutions in which notation is embedded in grammatical, punctuated sentences and the logical steps are signalled in words: introducing objects (let, suppose, define), stating quantifiers (for all, there exists), marking inference (hence, it follows that, since), naming the proof strategy (by contradiction, by induction, by the contrapositive) and closing the argument. Markers in mathematics expect the reasoning, not only the answer, to be readable, and students used to answer-only assessment often lose marks for unexplained steps.
masteryEvidence: Introduces every symbol before it is used and states its type or domain
Writes each displayed equation as part of a sentence, with connecting words and punctuation, and avoids starting a sentence with a symbol
Distinguishes necessary from sufficient conditions and 'if' from 'if and only if' in their own statements
Announces the proof strategy at the start and signals where each case or the inductive step begins and ends
Justifies each non-trivial step by citing a definition, earlier result or algebraic rule
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a correct but answer-only solution to a short proof (for example that the sum of two odd integers is even) written as a column of equations. Ask them to rewrite it as a proof a lecturer would accept. Check that they define the integers with appropriate quantifiers, link each line with words such as 'so' or 'hence', state the conclusion in words and punctuate the displayed lines as part of sentences.

topics.name: Working with concepts
topics.description: Handle contested social concepts (for example class, identity, power, inclusion, globalisation) explicitly: show that a concept is defined differently in different theoretical traditions, state and justify the definition adopted, and, in empirical work, operationalise it as indicators, measures or coding categories, or treat it as a sensitising concept in qualitative work. Markers in the social sciences reward conceptual precision and penalise treating contested terms as self-evident.
masteryEvidence: Shows that a key concept is contested by comparing at least two definitions from different sources or traditions
States the definition adopted for an assignment or study and justifies it in relation to the question
Translates a concept into observable indicators, survey items or coding categories and explains what they capture and miss
Uses the concept consistently in the sense adopted throughout the text
Distinguishes everyday uses of a term from its technical use in the field
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write an 80–120-word paragraph defining 'social exclusion' (or a key concept from their field) for an assignment. Check whether they acknowledge competing definitions with sources, select one with a reason linked to the task, and avoid dictionary definitions.

topics.name: Field notes, analytic memos and analysis accounts
topics.description: Produce the working and process texts of qualitative research: field notes that separate observational description from reflective and analytic comment; analytic memos that record developing codes, interpretations and questions; and accounts of the analysis process, for example in a methods chapter or appendix, that make coding and theme development transparent and position the researcher reflexively. Writing up findings, including the use of participant extracts, is covered by res.qualitative-reporting.
masteryEvidence: Writes field notes that separate concrete observation from interpretation and personal response, recording time, setting and context
Writes analytic memos that develop an interpretation of data, linking codes to emerging ideas and noting uncertainties and alternative readings
Describes the analysis process in enough detail for a reader to judge its rigour, avoiding the claim that themes simply 'emerged'
Explains analytic choices with reference to the approach used (for example reflexive thematic analysis) and its assumptions
Reflects in writing on how the researcher's position and decisions shaped the data and the analysis
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner a two-minute video of a public or classroom setting and ask for five minutes of field notes followed by a three-sentence analytic memo. Check whether the notes record observable detail with interpretation marked separately, and whether the memo develops a tentative interpretation linked to specific observations and notes a question for further analysis.

topics.name: Policy analysis
topics.description: Write academic analyses of public or educational policy: define and critically examine how a policy problem is framed, identify stakeholders and interests, assess the evidence base, compare policy options against explicit criteria such as effectiveness, equity, cost and feasibility, and reach a justified recommendation or critical conclusion. Policy analysis ranges from technical option appraisal to critical approaches that ask how problems are represented, and assignments may expect either.
masteryEvidence: Explains how a policy defines its problem and what alternative framings would imply
Identifies the main stakeholders and their interests
Evaluates the strength and transferability of the evidence cited for and against a policy
Compares at least two options against explicit criteria
Reaches a conclusion or recommendation that follows from the analysis and acknowledges trade-offs
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a one-page summary of a policy (for example a free school meals scheme) and ask for a 200-word critical paragraph. Check whether they examine how the problem is framed, refer to evidence and its limits, consider at least one alternative and avoid simply describing the policy or giving unsupported opinion.

topics.name: Justifying methodology
topics.description: Justify research design in writing: state the philosophical worldview or paradigm informing the study (for example post-positivist, constructivist, transformative or pragmatist), explain how the chosen approach and design follow from the research questions, justify sampling, data collection and analysis with reference to methodological literature, acknowledge trade-offs and ethical considerations, and distinguish methodology (the rationale) from methods (the procedures). Methodology chapters are where examiners judge coherence between questions, design and claims.
masteryEvidence: Links the chosen approach explicitly to the research questions and to a stated paradigm
Justifies each design decision (sampling, instruments, analysis) with a reason and, where appropriate, methodological citations
Acknowledges the main limitations of the design and explains why it was still the most appropriate choice
Distinguishes methodological rationale from procedural description
Uses paradigm terminology (ontology, epistemology, interpretivism) accurately and only where it does analytical work
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a research question and a methods paragraph that only describes procedures. Ask them to add three sentences of justification. Check whether the justification connects design to question, cites or names a methodological principle, and acknowledges a trade-off rather than claiming the design is simply 'best'.

topics.name: Laboratory notebooks and research records
topics.description: Keep contemporaneous, dated records of laboratory, computational or field work that another competent person could follow and that meet research-integrity and data-management expectations: aims and plans, materials and identifiers, procedures and any deviations from them, raw observations and measurements with units, file, sample and code locations, and brief interpretive comments kept distinguishable from observations. Notebooks, on paper or electronic, are a primary research record and are assessed in some practical modules and research projects, but their conventions are rarely taught explicitly.
masteryEvidence: Records each entry with a date, an aim and enough procedural detail, including deviations from the planned method, for another competent person to repeat the work
Records raw observations and measurements at the time, with units, uncertainties and sample or file identifiers, rather than reconstructing them later
Keeps observations, calculations and interpretive comments distinguishable, and corrects errors by annotation rather than deletion
Links entries to data files, code versions or samples so that results can be traced to their source
Explains why contemporaneous, unaltered records matter for reproducibility, data sharing and research integrity
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner a one-page notebook entry with a missing date, an unrecorded change to the method, a value without units and an overwritten result. Ask them to annotate what a supervisor or auditor would query and to rewrite two lines. Check whether they find all four problems, explain why each matters for reproducibility or integrity, and correct by annotation rather than by erasing.

topics.name: Writing clinical reasoning
topics.description: Make the reasoning behind clinical judgements explicit in assignments: move from a structured assessment of a patient or scenario to identifying and prioritising problems, to justified interventions and to how outcomes will be evaluated, linking each step to cues in the data, to evidence and to the relevant professional standards. Nursing, midwifery, pharmacy and allied-health assignments are marked on this visible reasoning, often scaffolded by a clinical reasoning cycle or a similar model, rather than on correct answers alone.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the relevant cues in a patient scenario and states what each may indicate, distinguishing data from inference
Prioritises problems or needs and gives an explicit reason for the order, such as risk or urgency
Justifies each proposed intervention by linking it to the assessment, to cited evidence and to professional standards or guidelines
States how and when the outcome will be evaluated and what would prompt a change of plan
Uses hedged and conditional language where the data are incomplete
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short patient scenario with observations and history, and ask for a 200-word paragraph explaining the priority problem and the first intervention. Check whether they cite specific cues from the scenario, explain why this problem takes priority, justify the intervention with evidence or a guideline, and hedge where the data are incomplete.

topics.name: Care plans
topics.description: Write care plans and care-planning assignments that move from a holistic assessment to prioritised, person-centred problems or needs, goals that are specific, measurable and time-bound, evidence-based interventions with rationales, and criteria and timing for evaluation. Care plans are usually structured by the nursing process (assessment, planning, implementation and evaluation, often with problem identification or nursing diagnosis as a separate step) and by the nursing model or documentation standard the programme specifies; they must be anonymised and use only approved abbreviations.
masteryEvidence: Derives each problem or need from documented assessment findings and orders the problems by an explicit priority
Writes goals as measurable, time-bound outcomes for the patient rather than as tasks for the practitioner
Links each intervention to a goal and gives a rationale supported by current evidence or guidance
States evaluation criteria and timescales that would show whether each goal has been met
Follows the programme's nursing model or template, uses approved abbreviations only and anonymises the patient
Uses respectful, person-centred language that reflects the patient's own priorities
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short assessment summary and ask for one row of a care plan (problem, goal, intervention with rationale, evaluation). Check whether the problem follows from the assessment, the goal is a measurable patient outcome with a timescale, the intervention is linked to the goal with an evidenced rationale, and the evaluation criterion measures the goal as worded.

topics.name: Language and genres of accounting and finance
topics.description: Read and write the genres of accounting and finance study: commentary on financial statements and ratios, audit, valuation and investment reports, and analyses of corporate disclosures. This requires reporting figures and changes accurately, moving from description to explanation and evaluation for a named user of the accounts, hedging forecasts and valuations to their assumptions, and reading corporate narratives critically, since narrative sections of annual reports are written to persuade as well as to inform.
masteryEvidence: Reports figures, ratios and year-on-year changes accurately, distinguishing percentage from percentage-point change and absolute from relative change
Moves from describing a financial result to explaining its likely drivers and evaluating its significance for a named user of the accounts
Hedges forecasts, valuations and recommendations by stating the assumptions on which they depend
Distinguishes audited figures from management commentary and identifies evaluative or promotional language in corporate narratives
Uses accounting terms precisely, recognising terms that differ between reporting frameworks or varieties of English (for example turnover and revenue, stock and inventory)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two years of summary figures for a company and a 100-word extract from its chair's statement, and ask for a 150-word commentary for an investor. Check whether figures and changes are reported accurately, the commentary explains and evaluates rather than only describes, forecasts are hedged to their assumptions, and the chair's evaluative claims are tested against the figures rather than repeated.

topics.name: Consultancy and client project reports
topics.description: Write reports for live or simulated consultancy projects in which a student team addresses a client organisation's problem: frame and agree the brief, present evidence-based analysis and prioritised, feasible recommendations with an implementation plan for the client, and, where required, a separate academic or reflective account for the marker. The genre serves two readers with different needs: a client who wants actionable advice in accessible language, and an academic marker who expects theory, evidence and critical reflection.
masteryEvidence: Restates the client's brief as a clearly framed problem with agreed scope, objectives and constraints
Orders findings and recommendations for the client, leading with the main recommendation in accessible language
Justifies each recommendation with evidence from the project and makes it actionable with responsibilities, timescale, cost or risk
Separates client-facing advice from the academic justification or reflection the marker requires, as the brief specifies
Evaluates the team's process and the client relationship in a reflective account supported by evidence and appropriate frameworks
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short client brief and a summary of project findings. Ask for the opening of an executive summary for the client and a 100-word paragraph for the marker explaining the basis of one recommendation. Check whether the client text leads with actionable recommendations in plain language, and whether the marker text justifies the recommendation with evidence and theory.

topics.name: Mooting and oral legal argument
topics.description: Prepare and deliver oral legal submissions in moots and other assessed advocacy exercises: draft a skeleton argument, order the grounds, cite authority orally in the conventions used in court, answer interventions from the bench, concede or distinguish where appropriate, and use the forms of address and register the court expects. Mooting is assessed on many LLB programmes and some LLMs, and judges reward responsiveness to questions as much as prepared delivery.
masteryEvidence: Drafts a skeleton argument that states each ground concisely with its supporting authorities
Presents submissions in a signposted order and cites authorities orally in the conventional spoken form, without reading out full citations
Answers a judge's intervention directly and then returns to the planned submission
Concedes a weak point or distinguishes an adverse authority without abandoning the overall case
Uses the forms of address and register appropriate to the court and keeps to a strict time limit
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner ten minutes to prepare a two-minute submission on one ground of a short moot problem, with two authorities, and interrupt once with a question from the bench. Check whether the submission is signposted, authorities are cited orally and used for a point, the question is answered directly before the learner resumes, and register and forms of address are appropriate.

topics.name: Legal research and dissertation writing
topics.description: Plan and write an LLB, LLM or doctoral law dissertation: choose and justify a method (doctrinal, socio-legal, comparative or theoretical), build a research question from a problem in the state of the law rather than only from an empirical gap, structure a sustained legal argument across chapters, and handle primary and secondary authority and note-based referencing such as OSCOLA at length. Doctrinal theses are rarely organised by IMRaD, so general research-writing models need adapting.
masteryEvidence: Formulates a research question that identifies a doctrinal problem, uncertainty or reform issue in the law
Names and justifies the method (doctrinal, socio-legal, comparative or theoretical) and explains how sources will be selected and analysed
Plans chapters so that each advances a stage of the argument rather than describing an area of law
Uses primary and secondary authority for their proper purposes consistently across a long text
Maintains accurate, consistent note-based referencing, a bibliography and tables of authorities across a dissertation
States the contribution of the dissertation, such as a reinterpretation, a reform proposal or a comparative insight, and its limits
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to bring a draft dissertation proposal or outline and to explain in five minutes the research question, method and chapter plan. Check whether the question identifies a legal problem rather than a topic, the method is named and justified, and each chapter has an argumentative function linked to the question.

topics.name: Psychology research reports
topics.description: Write empirical research reports in psychology in APA style: an introduction that reviews evidence and leads to explicit hypotheses; a method section reporting participants, design, materials and procedure in enough detail for replication; results reported with test statistics, effect sizes and confidence intervals in the conventional format; and a discussion that relates findings to the hypotheses and literature with calibrated claims. The report is the main assessed genre of psychology degrees, and its conventions are specified closely by the APA Publication Manual and departmental guides.
masteryEvidence: Writes an introduction that moves from theory and prior findings to a rationale and explicit, testable hypotheses
Reports participants, design, materials and procedure in enough detail for replication, including ethical approval and consent
Reports statistical results in APA format with test statistic, degrees of freedom, exact p values (or p < .001 for very small values), effect sizes and confidence intervals
Relates each finding to its hypothesis in the discussion and interprets non-significant results without claiming they show no effect
Describes participants in bias-free language following current APA guidance and the conventions of the field
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short statistics output and the hypothesis it tests, and ask for a results sentence and a two-sentence discussion comment. Check whether the result is reported in APA format with an effect size, the outcome is related to the hypothesis, and a non-significant result is interpreted without claiming that the null hypothesis has been proved.

topics.name: Education and TESOL practice genres
topics.description: Write the practice genres of education and TESOL programmes: lesson plans with a rationale that links aims, staging, activities and assessment to the learners and to theory; reflections on teaching practice that analyse taught or observed lessons and feedback; materials evaluations against explicit criteria; and reports of small-scale classroom research such as action research or practitioner enquiry. These genres connect teaching experience with research and theory and are central to assessment on initial teacher education and MA TESOL programmes.
masteryEvidence: Writes a lesson-plan rationale that justifies aims, staging and activities by reference to the learners and to relevant theory or research
Analyses a taught or observed lesson by linking specific classroom evidence to principles and proposing justified changes
Evaluates teaching materials against explicit, justified criteria rather than personal preference
Reports a small-scale classroom enquiry with a focused question, an appropriate and ethical design and claims scoped to the context
Uses prior teaching experience as evidence while relating it critically to the literature
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a one-page lesson plan without a rationale and a short description of the class, and ask for a 150-word rationale. Check whether the aims are justified by the learners' needs, at least one staging decision is linked to a named principle or study, and the writer anticipates a likely problem and how it will be handled.

topics.name: Practice-based research and exegesis
topics.description: Write the exegesis or critical commentary that accompanies practice-based or practice-led research in art, design and performance: situate the practice in its field and in relevant theory, articulate the research questions and methods pursued through making, document the process, and argue the contribution of the work and the text together. Institutions differ in how they weight practice and writing and in the expected length and form of the text, and the relationship between artefact and exegesis is itself debated.
masteryEvidence: Articulates the research question or concern that the practice addresses, rather than only describing the work
Situates the practice in relation to precedents, contemporary practitioners and relevant theory
Explains how making functioned as a method, documenting key decisions, iterations and turning points with visual evidence
Argues, with appropriate hedging, what the practice and text together contribute to knowledge or understanding in the field
Relates text and artefact explicitly, following the institution's rules on weighting and format
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to bring images of their work and a draft introduction to the exegesis. In a short conversation, ask what question the work investigates, which practitioners or theories it responds to, and what the work shows that was not known before. Check whether the written introduction states the question and context and makes a claim about contribution, rather than describing the work or the maker's biography.

dependencies.reason: Presenting and critiquing work in a crit requires describing and interpreting visual work with disciplinary vocabulary
Responding to critique in a crit extends general strategies for clarifying, answering and managing difficult questions
Giving and responding to critique depends on mitigated agreement and disagreement that preserve collegiality
Using crit feedback well requires appreciating feedback, managing affect and taking action, as in general feedback literacy
Statements describe and interpret the writer's own work, which draws on visual description and analysis
Statements authored by the artist or designer are usually written in the first person, which draws on control of self-mention
Statements work to tight word limits and depend on removing redundancy and empty phrases
A design rationale is built from explanations and justifications of decisions
Annotating and evaluating design development requires describing visual features precisely
Process documentation includes reflective commentary on what worked and what to change
Evaluating outcomes against the brief draws on criteria-based evaluation language
Visual analysis presupposes understanding how image, layout and colour make meaning alongside or instead of text
The core move in visual analysis is from description to analysis and interpretation
Describing composition uses spatial and part–whole language
Formal and art-historical analysis requires learning and using field-specific terms accurately
The business case report specialises the general case-study genre of applying concepts to a case and recommending action
