The analysis stage of a business case depends on applying management frameworks analytically rather than as lists
Cases include financial and market exhibits that must be interpreted in data commentary
Economic predictions from models are expressed as real and unreal conditionals
Comparative statics and policy analysis chain causal claims of varying strength
Empirical economics depends on distinguishing causal from correlational evidence and qualifying claims accordingly
Economic reasoning is often conducted through diagrams whose axes and curves must be read accurately
Memos, briefing notes and pitches adapt the decision-oriented structure of the business report to shorter formats
Pitches and briefings require analysing the audience's knowledge and decision before selecting content
Memos and briefing notes to managers require calibrating directness and face to role relationships
Using SWOT or Five Forces analytically is a specific case of applying concepts and models to a case
Acknowledging a framework's limitations draws on criteria for evaluating models such as scope and explanatory power
Evidence-based practice presupposes understanding of evidence types and hierarchies and their limits
Framing a focused clinical question in PICO form specialises the general skill of narrowing a topic into a searchable question
Judging the best available evidence requires consumer-level reading of effect sizes, confidence intervals and risk
Reflective practice writing in health specialises the general reflective genre (experience, analysis, future action) for professional standards and confidentiality
Analysis in health reflections is expected to draw on research evidence and professional guidance, not only personal response
Patient histories in case presentations depend on clear chronological sequencing and time expressions
Case presentations require accurate clinical terminology and conventional, locally approved abbreviations
Communicating with patients and senior colleagues depends on managing face, imposition and power distance
Explaining conditions and procedures to patients requires shifting from specialist to lay register
Checking patient understanding builds on general strategies for confirming and checking understanding in interaction
Placements expose students to regional and international accents and colloquial speech among patients and staff
Critical appraisal is the step of evidence-based practice that judges the validity and applicability of evidence
Written appraisal specialises the critical review of a single article, including its critical reading of samples, design, measures and limitations
Interpreting how language creates meaning depends on inferring implied meaning from textual detail
Close reading requires moving from describing what a text says to analysing how and interpreting why
Close reading is usually practised through purposeful annotation of a passage
Analysing diction requires sensitivity to differences in meaning, strength and connotation between near-synonyms
Working with primary sources presupposes the distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary sources
Sourcing a document involves recognising its author's position, interests and framing
Interpreting documents and images draws on close attention to their language and form
History and related fields often cite primary and archival sources in note-based systems such as Chicago notes
Interpretive essays are built from close analysis of textual evidence
The interpretive essay specialises thesis-led argument for interpretive claims
Textual evidence in the humanities is presented through short, grammatically integrated quotations with commentary
Reconstructing and assessing arguments requires understanding deductive validity and other forms of inference
The objection-and-reply structure of philosophy essays extends general rebuttal and concession
Setting out arguments in premise–conclusion form builds on diagramming argument structure
Philosophical writing depends on accurately reading dense primary philosophical texts
Much legal vocabulary consists of everyday words (consideration, action, party, hold) with specialised legal senses
Terms of art must be learned and used consistently as fixed technical terms
Legal register is best understood against a general model of how field, tenor and mode shape language
Recognising general academic Latin and abbreviations eases the learning of legal Latin and citation abbreviations
Judgments use terms of art and legal senses of common words that must be understood to extract the reasoning
Identifying the ratio requires locating the claims, reasons and conclusions in a judge's argument
Law reports follow conventional sections (headnote, facts, judgments) that support strategic reading
A case brief is a structured form of note-making from reading
Applying precedent to new facts requires knowing the ratio and material facts of decided cases
Problem questions are a legal form of applying general rules or concepts to a particular case
Many problem scenarios turn on statutory provisions as well as case law
Advice to a client must express the likely outcome with certainty matched to the strength of the legal analysis
Legislation uses deontic modals, defined terms and qualifying expressions with conventional legal meanings
Statutory sentences embed conditions and exceptions that must be parsed to find the main rule
Legislative provisions express conditions with if, unless, provided that and where, which must be read accurately
Legal essays argue from accurately understood authorities, which requires reading cases for ratio and reasoning
Legal essays specialise the thesis-led argumentative essay for legal authority and doctrine
Legal essays are normally referenced with OSCOLA footnotes, a note-based citation system
Legal reporting verbs (held, observed, submitted) carry specific meanings that extend general reporting-verb choice
Grammatical metaphor in scientific discourse is realised mainly through nominalisation, so learners must recognise and form process nouns before they can analyse its scientific function
Scientific technicality builds on the ability to learn, define and use field-specific terms consistently
Lexical density and the packaging of processes as things are easiest to grasp once the general contrast between spoken and written registers is understood
Scientific taxonomies are built with the language of classification (types, classes, criteria), which is usually taught first as a general rhetorical function
Scientific explanations depend on technical terms and nominalised causes to package each step of the mechanism
Causal, factorial and consequential explanations are built from cause–effect language of varying strength
Sequential explanations extend process description by adding causal links between ordered stages
Scientific explanations are usually co-presented with flow diagrams or cycles, and learners need language for describing these
Protocols are a procedural genre built on sequencing and purpose expressions from process description
Protocols and specifications are only usable if quantities, units and tolerances are stated in standard form
Specifications describe components and their functional relations, which draws on the language of structure and systems
Numbered steps and requirement lists need parallel form and list punctuation
Formulating testable hypotheses and predictions specialises the general language of predicting and hypothesising
Key experimental terms (error, control, significant, precise) are sub-technical words whose scientific sense differs from everyday use
Discussing uncertainty and significance assumes basic statistical vocabulary such as mean, range and standard deviation
Stating what results do and do not show within experimental uncertainty is a disciplinary application of calibrating claims to evidence
Installation and usage instructions and API contracts use the imperative steps and verifiable specification language developed in protocols and specifications
Useful comments and design rationales explain why a decision was taken, drawing on the language of explaining and justifying
Proof writing integrates equations, variables and symbols into prose, which requires reading and writing mathematical expressions in words
Proofs are deductive arguments, and proof by induction or contradiction presupposes understanding of deductive inference
Theorems and proof steps are typically conditional statements whose exact form (if, only if, if and only if) carries the logic
Signalling inference steps (hence, thus, since, conversely) depends on precise use of logical connectors
Working with contested concepts extends formal, operational and contested definition from the general function of defining
Key social science concepts (culture, power, class) are sub-technical words whose disciplinary sense differs from everyday use
Showing that a concept is contested involves writing relationships of agreement and difference between sources' definitions
Accounts of analysis make sense only against the paradigm and design of the study, which shape what counts as a transparent account
Field notes, memos and accounts of analysis position the researcher in relation to the data, which requires understanding reflexivity
Policy analysis is organised around problem definition, options and evaluation, extending situation–problem–response–evaluation patterns
Critical policy analysis requires surfacing the assumptions and values built into how a problem is framed
Assessing a policy's evidence base requires knowing the strengths and limits of different kinds of evidence
Stakeholder analysis requires representing different interests and perspectives fairly
Methodology justification extends the general methods-section genre with paradigm-level rationale
Design choices are justified by their fit with the research questions, which must already be formulated
Discussing paradigms presupposes an evaluativist understanding of knowledge as constructed and contested
The assessment and plan that close a case presentation summarise clinical reasoning that the presenter must be able to make explicit
Case presentations are shaped for a particular audience and purpose, such as a ward round, a handover or a teaching session
Judging the results of a study requires interpreting effect sizes, confidence intervals and p values
Field notes and memos depend on keeping description distinguishable from analysis and interpretation
Writing field notes in real time extends the note-taking skill of deciding what to record
Statements are written for specific readers, such as exhibition visitors or admissions tutors, whose knowledge shapes how much context and theory to include
Raw measurements are usable as a research record only if quantities, units and uncertainties are written correctly at the time
Notebook entries record the protocol followed and any deviations from it, which requires reading protocols precisely
Entries state aims, variables and conditions and note sources of error in the language of experimental design
Conventions such as dated, unaltered and attributable entries exist to prevent and detect fabrication and falsification, so they make sense once research integrity is understood
Justifying interventions requires integrating appraised evidence with clinical expertise and patient preferences, the core of evidence-based practice
Clinical reasoning writing is built from explanations and justifications of each judgement
Judgements made from incomplete clinical data must be stated with certainty matched to the evidence
Linking a patient's presentation to physiological or theoretical knowledge applies general concepts to a particular case
A care plan records the outcome of clinical reasoning, from assessment cues to prioritised problems, goals, interventions and evaluation
Care plans require accurate clinical terminology and only locally approved abbreviations
Person-centred care plans depend on respectful person-first or identity-first wording that follows professional conventions
Financial statement commentary is a form of data commentary that highlights, explains and evaluates figures
Reporting financial performance depends on distinguishing absolute, relative and percentage-point change
Forecasts and valuations must be hedged to the assumptions and uncertainty on which they rest
Reading corporate narratives critically requires recognising the writer's interests and persuasive framing
The consultancy report adapts the problem-oriented business report, with findings and recommendations for a decision-maker
Analysing a client's situation draws on the problem definition and option evaluation practised in business case analysis
Clients often read only the executive summary, which must stand alone and lead with recommendations
Many consultancy modules require a reflective account of the project and the team process
Each moot ground applies legal authority to the facts of a problem and anticipates the other side, as in written problem answers
Moot submissions are a formal, adversarial form of arguing orally
Answering interventions from the bench extends general strategies for handling questions
Forms of address, concession and disagreement with the bench depend on managing face and formality
A law dissertation sustains the authority-based argument of the legal essay across a much longer text
Building a legal research question adapts general skills of formulating aims and questions to doctrinal problems
Planning chapters requires knowing the macrostructures available to long research texts and adapting them to legal argument
Legal research depends on finding and updating authorities in legal databases
The psychology report is the discipline’s realisation of the experimental laboratory report
Results sections require reporting statistics, effect sizes and tables in conventional formats
Hypotheses, variables and controls in psychology studies use the language of experimental design
Psychology reports use APA author–date citation throughout
Teaching-practice reflections specialise the general reflective genre for classroom experience
Lesson rationales and materials evaluations apply theories of learning and teaching to a particular class or text
Materials evaluation depends on criteria-based evaluation of strengths and weaknesses
Classroom research reports must justify their design and data collection, often within a practitioner-enquiry approach
Documenting and justifying decisions through the process is the basis of the account of making as method
Articulating concept and context concisely for a body of work prepares for the longer contextualising argument
Situating practice in its field adapts the positioning work of the literature review to practitioners, works and theory
The exegesis must claim the contribution of practice and text together, which draws on general skills of claiming contribution
Analysis in placement reflections is expected to make clinical judgements and their justification explicit

guidance.summary: Dannels (2005) analysed design crits as a genre with characteristic roles and performances that students learn largely through participation, which means the expectations stay tacit for newcomers. Schön's (1983) account of a design tutor and student working through a project shows critique as reflection-in-action carried out through talk and drawing. For multilingual students, difficulties often arise from figurative and evaluative studio vocabulary, from the public nature of critique and from different expectations about challenging a tutor. Teaching should make the structure and language of crits explicit, rehearse them in low-stakes settings and, ideally, observe real crits with tutors.

activities.title: Anatomy of a crit
learnerActions: Watch or observe a recorded or live crit, with permission
Note the stages (presentation, questions, critique, response, summary) and who speaks when
Collect phrases tutors use to praise, question and suggest, and discuss their likely meaning with a tutor or peer
activities.intendedInsight: Crits follow recognisable patterns and use a specialised evaluative vocabulary that can be learned.
activities.rationale: Treating the crit as a genre with roles and stages, as Dannels does, makes its tacit conventions available for explicit teaching.

activities.title: Rehearsed mini-crits
learnerActions: Prepare a two-minute presentation of a current piece of work covering intention, process and one key decision
Present to a small group, who each ask one question and give one specific suggestion
Respond to each comment, then note one action for the next iteration
activities.intendedInsight: Critique is part of the design process, and responding thoughtfully is a skill, not a test of the work's worth.
activities.rationale: Schön describes design learning as reflective dialogue about work in progress, and low-stakes rehearsal builds the confidence to take part in it.

difficulties.pattern: Not understanding figurative studio language ('It needs to breathe', 'It doesn't resolve') and nodding along.
difficulties.revealedBy: Students who do not act on crit feedback or who report that feedback was unclear.
difficulties.response: Build a class glossary of studio expressions with tutors, and practise clarification questions. Encourage asking during the crit.

difficulties.pattern: Feeling that critique of my work is critique of me, and staying silent or defending every choice.
difficulties.revealedBy: Defensive or minimal responses in crits, and distress afterwards.
difficulties.response: Discuss the purpose of crits and practise separating work from self. Recognise that crits can be uncomfortable; do not dismiss these feelings.

difficulties.pattern: In my previous studies the tutor’s judgement was final, so I accept every comment and change the work without explaining my choices.
difficulties.revealedBy: Work that changes direction after every crit, and tutors' comments that the student does not explain or defend decisions.
difficulties.response: Make explicit that crits usually expect students to explain and argue for their decisions, and that tutors’ comments are often offered as provocations rather than instructions. Model respectful ways to explain a choice. Tutors can help by saying which comments are suggestions and which are requirements.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to present a piece of work for two minutes and respond to one critical comment and one vague comment.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains intentions and decisions concisely, asks for clarification of the vague comment, and responds to criticism with reasoning or openness to development.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Presents clearly but accepts or rejects criticism without reasoning, or does not seek clarification.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the process chronologically and does not engage with comments.

guidance.contextNotes: On foundation art and design courses, crits are frequent and formative, so early support helps. On pre-sessional pathways, simulated crits prepare students. UG and PGT students face assessed reviews and final crits, sometimes with external critics, where both language and confidence matter.
reviewNotes: Crit formats and their assessment role vary widely across institutions and between art and design disciplines.
The skeleton types this topic as SOCIOPRAGMATIC; Dannels treats crits as a genre, and either framing is defensible.

guidance.summary: Artist and design statements are short, hybrid genres that inform about a work while promoting the artist or designer, combining description, explanation and self-presentation in a way similar to the promotional professional genres analysed by Bhatia (1993). There is little linguistic research on them, so teaching should rely on analysing a range of statements for different purposes, with tutors, and on the principle that concrete description of the work grounds abstract claims. Kress and van Leeuwen (2006) offer vocabulary for describing visual choices precisely.

activities.title: Statements for different readers
learnerActions: Collect three statements written for different purposes (exhibition label, degree show, application)
Compare their length, opening move, balance of description and concept, and register
Write two versions of a statement about your own work for two different readers
activities.intendedInsight: A statement's content and register depend on its purpose and reader.
activities.rationale: Comparing realisations of a genre across purposes reflects Bhatia's account of how communicative purpose shapes professional genres.

activities.title: Ground the abstract
learnerActions: Underline abstract claims in a draft statement
For each, add a sentence describing a visible feature of the work that supports it
Delete any abstract claim you cannot support with something visible or a specific process
activities.intendedInsight: Abstract claims about a work persuade only when tied to concrete, visible features.
activities.rationale: Linking claims to specific visual choices draws on visual grammar to give learners precise descriptive resources.

difficulties.pattern: Imitating the abstract, theory-heavy language of published statements to sound professional.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements full of abstract nouns and theoretical terms with little reference to the work itself.
difficulties.response: Discuss when theoretical language helps and when it obscures, and use the grounding activity. Present this as a debated style in the art world, not a fixed rule.

difficulties.pattern: Describing my life story or the whole making process instead of the work.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements that are mainly biographical or chronological accounts of making.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to start with what the work is and what it explores, and to select only process details that illuminate it.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a 100-word statement about one of their works (or a provided image) for an exhibition visitor.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Opens with what the work is and explores, describes it concretely, links it to one context and uses accessible language.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Explains the concept but describes the work vaguely or relies on abstract terms.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Biographical or purely emotional account with no description of the work.

guidance.contextNotes: On foundation courses, short statements accompany portfolios for degree applications. On pre-sessional art and design pathways, they are a useful short-writing task, and PG entrants can practise statements about an existing body of work. UG and PGT students write statements for degree shows and exhibitions, and PGT statements are expected to engage more with context and theory; the longer research text of practice-based degrees is covered by dad.practice-research-exegesis.
reviewNotes: There is little applied linguistic research on artist statements; guidance draws on genre theory and practice and should be reviewed with art and design staff.

guidance.summary: Schön (1983) describes design as a reflective conversation with the situation, in which designers make moves, see what results and reframe the problem. Rationales and process documentation are the written trace of that conversation. Cross (2011) synthesises research on how designers work, including the co-evolution of problem and solution, which helps explain why rationales should show iteration and rejected options rather than a straight path. Because rationales are multimodal, Kress and van Leeuwen (2006) are useful for the relation between annotation and image. Expectations vary between design disciplines, so local exemplars are essential.

activities.title: What to why
learnerActions: Read annotations from a sketchbook or process board
Classify each as describing what was done or explaining why
Rewrite the 'what' annotations so that they explain the reason for the change with reference to the brief or users
activities.intendedInsight: Process documentation is valued for the reasoning it reveals, not as a record of activity.
activities.rationale: Making design reasoning explicit reflects Schön's account of design moves and their evaluation.

activities.title: The road not taken
learnerActions: Choose a key decision in your project
Present two alternatives you considered, with images, and the criteria you used to choose
Write a short paragraph explaining the decision and one compromise it involved
activities.intendedInsight: Showing rejected alternatives demonstrates design judgement.
activities.rationale: Design research describes problem and solution as evolving together, so documenting alternatives shows the process assessors want to see.

difficulties.pattern: Presenting the process as a straight line to the final design, hiding failures.
difficulties.revealedBy: Rationales that show only successful steps, with feedback asking for evidence of iteration or experimentation.
difficulties.response: Explain that assessors value iteration and learning from failure, and show exemplars that document dead ends.

difficulties.pattern: Annotations that label rather than explain ('Final colour scheme').
difficulties.revealedBy: Sketchbooks with many images and minimal reasoning.
difficulties.response: Use the what-to-why activity and require each annotation to contain a reason.

diagnostic.task: Give three development images and ask the learner to write annotations and a short rationale for the final choice.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Annotations explain reasons tied to the brief or users, and the rationale compares alternatives and acknowledges a limitation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Annotations describe changes clearly but give few reasons, or the rationale ignores alternatives.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Labels images or describes personal preference without reasoning.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation students build sketchbook practice. UG design students produce process documentation for every project. PGT students write more extended rationales that connect practice to research and theory.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with grp.technical-design-report (engineering) in purpose; design rationales in art and design are more visual and reflective.

guidance.summary: Kress and van Leeuwen (2006) provide a grammar of visual design (representational, interactive and compositional meanings, including information value, salience and framing) that gives learners precise, teachable categories for analysis. Rose (2016) frames visual analysis around the sites of production, the image itself and its audiences, which helps learners move from formal description to contextual interpretation. Art history and design disciplines also use their own formal vocabulary, so teaching should combine these frameworks with the terminology the department uses.

activities.title: Describe before you interpret
learnerActions: Look at an image for two minutes and list only what is visible
Organise the list by composition (where things are), salience (what stands out) and colour or tone
Write an analysis paragraph that moves from two described features to a hedged interpretation
activities.intendedInsight: Strong visual analysis is grounded in careful, systematic description.
activities.rationale: Kress and van Leeuwen's compositional categories give a systematic basis for description that supports interpretation.

activities.title: Same image, three sites
learnerActions: Choose an image or design from your field
In groups, discuss its production (who, how, why), the image itself, and how different audiences might read it
Write a paragraph interpreting the image that draws on at least two of these sites
activities.intendedInsight: Meaning depends on context of production and reception as well as on what is in the image.
activities.rationale: Rose's sites of meaning support moving from formal analysis to critical interpretation.

difficulties.pattern: Writing what I like or dislike about the image rather than analysing it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Analyses dominated by personal preference and evaluative adjectives (beautiful, interesting).
difficulties.response: Separate personal response from analysis explicitly, and require evidence from visible features for any evaluative claim.

difficulties.pattern: Lacking the vocabulary for spatial and formal description, and relying on vague words.
difficulties.revealedBy: Descriptions that use 'thing', 'some colours' or 'on the side', and short analyses.
difficulties.response: Build a word bank for composition, colour and texture, and practise information-gap description in which a partner draws from the description.

diagnostic.task: Show an unfamiliar image and ask for a 150-word analysis.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Systematic description with accurate vocabulary, links between at least two formal features and meaning, hedged interpretation and some reference to context.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate description but little interpretation, or interpretation without visual evidence.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Personal opinion or a narrative of what the image shows.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional pathways, focus on description vocabulary and the move to interpretation. UG students use visual analysis in contextual studies essays and crits. PGT students apply theoretical frameworks to interpretation.

guidance.summary: Nathan's (2013) genre analysis of the business case report describes a problem-oriented structure that differs from the essay: the writer identifies a problem, analyses it, evaluates alternatives and makes recommendations for an organisational reader. Zhu (2004) found that business courses assign a range of such case-based and professional tasks requiring skills beyond the essay. Teaching should start from exemplars and briefs in the student's own school, because schools vary in how far they expect headings, theory and personal recommendation, and should involve subject staff in setting and reviewing tasks.

activities.title: Problem or symptom?
learnerActions: Read a short case and list everything that is going wrong
Sort the list into symptoms and underlying problems, using arrows to show which causes which
Write a one-sentence problem statement and compare it with other groups
activities.intendedInsight: A strong case analysis is built on a well-defined problem, which is usually a cause rather than the most visible symptom.
activities.rationale: Problem identification is the opening move of the business case report as described by Nathan, and sorting symptoms from causes makes that move explicit.

activities.title: Options against criteria
learnerActions: Generate three options for the problem identified
Agree four criteria (for example cost, time, risk, strategic fit) and score each option in a decision matrix
Write the evaluation and recommendation section from the matrix, then compare with a high-scoring exemplar
activities.intendedInsight: Recommendations are persuasive when they follow visibly from an evaluation against criteria.
activities.rationale: Making evaluation criteria explicit supports the option-evaluation and recommendation stages that distinguish case reports from discussion essays.

difficulties.pattern: Retelling the case in detail before any analysis, as if the marker had not read it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Case reports in which a third or more of the word count summarises the case narrative.
difficulties.response: Clarify that the reader knows the case and wants analysis. Set a strict limit for background and show exemplars. Do not ban background entirely; a short framing of the problem is expected.

difficulties.pattern: Recommendations that do not follow from the analysis, or that are generic (improve marketing, train staff).
difficulties.revealedBy: Recommendation sections that introduce new ideas or could apply to any company.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to link each recommendation to a numbered finding and to add who, what, when and cost. Use the decision matrix to make the link visible.

diagnostic.task: Give a one-page case and ask for an outline of a case report: problem statement, three analytic points with evidence, two options and a recommendation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Defines a causal problem, supports analysis with case data, evaluates options against criteria and recommends one with implementation notes.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies a problem and recommends a solution but the analysis is a list of facts or the options are not evaluated.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the case and offers general opinions.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional business pathways, use short cases and contrast the case report with the essay; UG entrants need the basic problem–analysis–recommendation pattern, while PG entrants should practise it under time pressure. In UG in-sessional work, use the module’s own case and brief. PGT students on intensive programmes meet many cases quickly, so focus on efficient problem definition and recommendation writing.
reviewNotes: The overlap with grp.case-study is handled by treating that topic as the general genre and this one as its business-school realisation.

guidance.summary: McCloskey (1998) argued that economics is rhetorical: it persuades through models, metaphors and stylised assumptions as well as through data, which makes the language of models a legitimate object of teaching. For learners, the key resources are conditional and ceteris paribus structures, comparative statics, the precise description of diagrams and the positive–normative distinction. Because economics varies from highly mathematical to more discursive (for example in political economy), the teacher should check with lecturers which kind of writing the module expects.

activities.title: Holding everything else constant
learnerActions: Read three short predictions from an economics textbook and underline the assumptions, conditions and ceteris paribus clauses
Rewrite each prediction without its assumptions and discuss what claim it now makes
Write your own prediction about a change in one variable, stating assumptions explicitly
activities.intendedInsight: Economic predictions are conditional on stated assumptions, and dropping them changes the claim.
activities.rationale: Making the assumptions and conditions of model-based argument explicit reflects McCloskey's account of economic reasoning as built from models with stylised assumptions.

activities.title: Diagram to prose
learnerActions: Work in pairs: one student describes a change in a supply-and-demand or cost diagram while the other draws it without seeing the original
Compare drawings and identify which words caused errors (shift, movement along, increase in demand, increase in quantity demanded)
Write a short paragraph explaining the change and its effect on equilibrium
activities.intendedInsight: Precise distinctions such as shift versus movement along encode different economic events.
activities.rationale: Information-gap description exposes ambiguity in the learner's language through a listener's misunderstanding.

difficulties.pattern: Mixing normative judgements into positive analysis ('The government should not tax this because demand will fall').
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers to explain-type questions that drift into opinion, with feedback about relevance or objectivity.
difficulties.response: Classify sentences as positive or normative and discuss where each belongs in an answer. Normative argument is legitimate when the question asks for evaluation.

difficulties.pattern: Treating model predictions as unconditional facts about the real economy.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements such as 'Price will rise' with no assumptions or conditions, or confusion when real data diverge from the model.
difficulties.response: Have learners add the assumptions and conditions to each prediction and discuss what happens when they do not hold.

difficulties.pattern: Using 'cause' or 'lead to' for relationships found only in correlational data.
difficulties.revealedBy: Empirical essays that overclaim causation from regression results or descriptive statistics.
difficulties.response: Contrast sentences that report association and causation, and connect this to what research designs can support.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain in writing the effect of a fall in consumer income on the market for a normal good, using a diagram.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the assumption of a normal good, shows a shift of the demand curve, explains the effects on price and quantity with ceteris paribus, and avoids normative comment.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the correct direction of change but confuses shift and movement along, or omits conditions.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives a general opinion about recession without model-based reasoning.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional economics pathways, focus on basic model language and diagram description for UG entrants and on reading empirical economics for PG entrants. In UG in-sessional work, link the topic to essay and exam answers. At PGT, the emphasis shifts to empirical claims, econometric reporting and the hedging of causal claims.
reviewNotes: ESP research on economics discourse could support this topic further; the guidance currently draws mainly on McCloskey (1998) and general work on causal and conditional language.

guidance.summary: Bhatia (1993) shows how professional genres such as promotional and business letters are shaped by communicative purpose and by the relationship between writer and reader, and Zhu (2004) found that business courses assign memos, letters, reports and similar tasks that mimic workplace writing. Teaching should therefore contrast these genres with the essay: the main point first, organisation for a decision-maker, and tone fitted to role relationships. Because company and school templates differ, learners should analyse the specific brief, template and exemplars.

activities.title: Essay to memo
learnerActions: Read a short academic answer to a business question
Identify the recommendation and the two strongest reasons
Rewrite the content as a memo to a named manager, with the recommendation in the first sentence, and compare tone across the class
activities.intendedInsight: The same content is reorganised and re-voiced when the reader changes from marker to decision-maker.
activities.rationale: Rewriting across genres highlights how purpose and reader shape structure, as genre analysis of professional writing predicts.

activities.title: Pitch in three minutes
learnerActions: Analyse a recorded or transcribed pitch for its stages (problem, solution, benefits, evidence, request)
Plan a three-minute pitch for a product or project from your module using the same stages
Deliver the pitch and receive peer feedback on clarity of the request and evidence
activities.intendedInsight: A pitch is a persuasive genre with a predictable structure that ends in a specific request.
activities.rationale: Move analysis of a model before production applies genre pedagogy to a spoken professional genre that business schools assess.

difficulties.pattern: Writing memos and briefing notes as essays, with background first and the recommendation in the last paragraph.
difficulties.revealedBy: Memos marked down for structure or for burying the main point.
difficulties.response: Contrast reader needs in each genre and practise front-loading. Do not suggest that the essay structure is wrong; it suits a different purpose.

difficulties.pattern: Being very indirect or very blunt with a senior reader in a simulated workplace task.
difficulties.revealedBy: Memos that are either heavily mitigated and unclear or directive in a way that suits a superior rather than a subordinate.
difficulties.response: Discuss the role relationship in the brief and model wording at different levels of directness. Treat expectations as local business conventions, not universal norms.

diagnostic.task: Give a 300-word essay paragraph on a business issue and ask for a 120-word memo to a line manager recommending action.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Opens with purpose and recommendation, gives concise reasons, closes with a next step, and uses a tone suitable for a manager.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Shortens the text but keeps the essay order or an unsuitable tone.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the paragraph without a clear recommendation or reader orientation.

guidance.contextNotes: UG business students meet these genres in modules on management and communication. PGT students, especially on MBA-type programmes, are often assessed through reports, pitches and briefing papers, and some will already know workplace conventions from experience that may differ from the school's expectations.
reviewNotes: 'Bottom line up front' ordering is a widely taught convention, but expectations vary between organisations, sectors and countries; it is presented as typical for assessed business-school memos.

Review response (R1-34): the topic is kept as one topic for memos, briefing notes, management reports and pitches, which share a reader-first, decision-oriented logic and are usually taught together; the consultancy report and accounting and finance genres are now separate topics (dbe.consultancy-report, dbe.accounting-finance-discourse).

guidance.summary: Management frameworks are useful prompts, but Hill and Westbrook (1997), studying SWOT use in companies, found that outputs tended to be long, unprioritised lists that were rarely used in later strategy work. That is the same pattern markers criticise in student work. Teaching should frame each framework as a means to an analytic end: select, evidence, prioritise and draw implications. Nathan (2013) shows that the analysis stage of the business case report is where such frameworks are expected to do this work.

activities.title: From list to analysis
learnerActions: Take an unprioritised SWOT or PESTLE table for a familiar company
Delete factors that lack evidence and rank the remainder by likely impact
Write a paragraph on the two most significant factors, explaining their implications and how internal and external factors interact
activities.intendedInsight: A framework produces analysis only when its contents are evidenced, prioritised and connected to a decision.
activities.rationale: Hill and Westbrook's finding that SWOT outputs are rarely prioritised or used shows why the move from list to implication is the teaching target.

activities.title: Choosing the right tool
learnerActions: Read three short case questions (for example entering a new market, improving internal efficiency, responding to a new competitor)
Decide which framework fits each question best and why
Write one sentence for each acknowledging what the chosen framework cannot capture
activities.intendedInsight: Frameworks answer different questions, and choosing one is itself an analytical decision with limitations.
activities.rationale: Justifying framework choice and limits reflects the evaluative use of frameworks expected in the analysis stage of case reports.

difficulties.pattern: Including every framework taught in the module to show knowledge.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reports with several framework tables but little analysis, and feedback such as 'descriptive' or 'lacks depth'.
difficulties.response: Show markers' criteria and high-scoring exemplars that use one or two frameworks in depth. Discuss depth versus breadth.

difficulties.pattern: Listing factors as bullet points without evidence or implications.
difficulties.revealedBy: Framework tables with generic entries that could apply to any company.
difficulties.response: Require each factor to have a piece of evidence from the case and a 'so what' sentence. Avoid simply asking for more factors.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a 150-word PESTLE-based paragraph on one external factor affecting a company described in a short case.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Selects a significant factor, supports it with case evidence and explains its implication for the company's decision.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies a relevant factor but gives generic evidence or no implication.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists several PESTLE categories with one-line entries and no analysis.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional business pathways should introduce the analytical use of frameworks early, with short cases. UG students meet many frameworks across modules and need help to use them selectively. PGT management students, some of whom have used frameworks at work, are assessed heavily on them and need to adjust to academic expectations of critique, evidence and prioritisation.

guidance.summary: Sackett et al. (1996) define evidence-based medicine as combining the best current research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values, and explicitly reject the caricature of it as 'cookbook' practice. Health students often meet the concept through evidence hierarchies alone, so teaching should restore all three components and show how they surface in assignment language. Greenhalgh (2019) gives an accessible account of question framing and appraisal, including the point that the type of question determines the kind of evidence needed, and Gigerenzer et al. (2007) show why understanding how risk is expressed is part of using evidence well. Current guideline methods also grade the certainty of a body of evidence (for example with the GRADE approach) rather than ranking study designs in a single pyramid.

activities.title: Three-way decision
learnerActions: Read a short scenario in which research, clinical experience and patient preference point in different directions
In groups, list what each source of evidence contributes and what its limits are
Write a recommendation paragraph that integrates all three and compare it with a model written by a clinical lecturer
activities.intendedInsight: Evidence-based practice is a judgement that integrates research, expertise and patient values, and writing must show that integration.
activities.rationale: Working from Sackett et al.'s definition counters the narrower reading of evidence-based practice as following the highest-ranked study, and makes the expected argument structure explicit.

activities.title: From scenario to question
learnerActions: Read three brief clinical scenarios, one about an intervention and two about patients’ experiences or the meaning of a condition
Decide what type of question each raises and frame it with a suitable framework, such as PICO for the intervention question and PEO or SPIDER for the experience questions
Turn each question into search terms and discuss which study designs would best answer it
activities.intendedInsight: The type of question determines both the framing tool and the kind of evidence needed, which is one limitation of a single hierarchy.
activities.rationale: Question framing is the first step in evidence-based practice as described in the clinical literature; matching the framework to the question type prevents qualitative questions being forced into an intervention format.

difficulties.pattern: Evidence-based means the strongest study wins. If there is an RCT, that settles it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Assignments that recommend interventions solely on the basis of trial results, with no discussion of context or patient perspective.
difficulties.response: Return to the three components and to examples where patient values or context change the decision. Show markers' comments that reward integration.

difficulties.pattern: Citing guidelines and textbooks as if they were primary evidence, or citing a source because it is authoritative rather than because of its evidence base.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reference lists dominated by textbooks and policy documents in assignments that ask for research evidence.
difficulties.response: Show the difference between a guideline, the studies it synthesises, and a textbook summary, and agree with subject staff what each assignment expects. Avoid framing the learner's earlier practice as wrong; treat it as a different convention.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain, in about 100 words, what evidence-based practice means and to give one example of when the best research evidence might not determine a decision.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names research evidence, clinical expertise and patient values and gives a plausible example where values or context shift the decision.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Defines it as using research evidence and mentions patients only in passing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Equates it with using any published source or with following guidelines.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional health pathways, introduce the three components of evidence-based practice and question framing with simple scenarios; for PG entrants who are experienced practitioners, focus on expressing professional judgement in academic terms. In UG in-sessional work, link the concept to assignment argument, question framing for literature reviews and referencing. Many PGT health students are experienced practitioners for whom the focus is on articulating tacit expertise and engaging with graded certainty of evidence rather than with a single hierarchy.
reviewNotes: Terminology varies (evidence-based medicine, practice, nursing, healthcare); the topic uses evidence-based practice as the umbrella term.
The GRADE approach is mentioned as context, but no GRADE source is in the bibliography.

guidance.summary: Reflective writing in health draws on Schön's (1983) account of reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action and is usually scaffolded with models such as Gibbs's (1988) cycle or the What? So what? Now what? questions (originating with Borton and developed by Driscoll and by Rolfe et al., 2001). Models help, but used mechanically they produce long descriptions and superficial analysis. Ryan (2011) proposes making the language of deeper reflection explicit: shifts from past-tense report to present-tense analysis that draws on theory, and to future-oriented action. Programmes differ in the model they require and in the use of first person, so check the brief and use local exemplars.

activities.title: Weighing the stages
learnerActions: Read two anonymised reflections on the same type of placement incident, one high-scoring and one low-scoring
Highlight the description, feelings, analysis and action-plan stages in different colours and estimate the proportion of each
Identify the language that marks analysis (because, this may reflect, according to) and the sources each writer uses
Revise the low-scoring reflection's analysis paragraph
activities.intendedInsight: Marks are earned in analysis and action planning, and analysis uses different language and draws on literature.
activities.rationale: Comparing high- and low-rated texts makes the valued features visible, and attention to tense and evidential language follows Ryan's social semiotic approach.

activities.title: From feeling to explanation
learnerActions: Write three sentences describing how you felt during a challenging communication on placement or in study
For each feeling, write a 'so what' sentence that explains it using a concept, standard or piece of research
Add a 'now what' sentence for each that names a specific, observable change
activities.intendedInsight: In professional reflection, feelings are data to be explained, not the conclusion.
activities.rationale: The What? So what? Now what? structure directs the writer from experience to meaning and action, which is where professional reflection is assessed.

difficulties.pattern: Following the model stage by stage with equal weight, so that description and feelings take most of the word count.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reflections that are long on narrative and short on analysis, with feedback such as 'too descriptive'.
difficulties.response: Set word budgets for each stage and use exemplars to show typical proportions. Do not ban description; it should be selective and serve the analysis.

difficulties.pattern: Writing about personal mistakes feels unsafe or inappropriate, so I present everything as positive.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reflections with no acknowledged difficulty or learning, or with vague statements of improvement.
difficulties.response: Discuss the professional purpose of reflection and the programme's guidance on what is safe to disclose. Model professional, measured self-evaluation, and respect that comfort with self-disclosure varies with prior schooling and individual experience.

difficulties.pattern: Identifying patients, staff or wards, or describing them in judgemental terms.
difficulties.revealedBy: Names, dates, locations or evaluative descriptions of colleagues in draft reflections.
difficulties.response: Teach anonymisation conventions and professional language explicitly, with reference to the programme's confidentiality policy.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a 200-word reflection on a short scenario, using the model their programme requires.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Brief anonymised description, analysis that explains the event with reference to a concept or standard, and a specific action plan, with appropriate tense shifts.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Follows the stages but analysis is limited to personal feelings, or the action plan is generic.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Narrative account of the event with an evaluative conclusion and no analysis.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional health pathways, introduce reflection as a genre and its tense and stance patterns. UG nursing, midwifery and allied health students write reflections from the first placement onwards; teach early that, following UK regulators' joint guidance on reflective practice, reflective accounts should be anonymised and focused on learning rather than on a detailed factual record, because they are not legally privileged. PGT practitioners may need help to make reflection analytical and to link it to advanced practice literature.
reviewNotes: Use of particular reflective models (Gibbs, Driscoll, Johns, Rolfe et al.) varies by programme; the topic is model-neutral.

guidance.summary: Case presentations are genres in which the selection and order of information support clinical reasoning. Lingard et al. (2003) found that students’ case presentations were shaped by a tension between school expectations (completeness, display of knowledge) and workplace expectations (relevance to the clinical problem), so teaching should make the decision-making purpose explicit. Nesi and Gardner (2012) identify the case study as a genre family in which health students apply professional knowledge to a specific case, and written case presentations share that purpose. Formats differ between professions, specialties and institutions, so local templates and exemplars are essential.

activities.title: What matters for this patient?
learnerActions: Receive a full set of notes on a fictional patient
Decide which details are essential, useful or irrelevant for a presentation focused on the presenting problem
Give a two-minute presentation in the conventional order and receive feedback on selection and ordering
activities.intendedInsight: A case presentation selects information for a clinical purpose; completeness is not the goal.
activities.rationale: Selection for relevance addresses the school–workplace tension Lingard et al. describe in student case presentations.

activities.title: Same patient, different audience
learnerActions: Prepare a full written case presentation from a set of notes on a fictional patient
Cut it to a one-minute ward-round version, deciding what must stay
Explain to a partner what you removed and why that audience did not need it
activities.intendedInsight: The same case is presented differently for different purposes, and deciding what to leave out is a clinical judgement.
activities.rationale: Lingard et al. show that workplace audiences value relevance to the clinical problem over completeness; compressing a presentation for a named audience practises that judgement.

difficulties.pattern: Including everything known about the patient to show thoroughness.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long presentations with the presenting problem buried, and feedback asking 'what is the point?'.
difficulties.response: Show model presentations with a clear clinical focus and discuss how relevance is decided. Bring in a clinical educator to explain what supervisors listen for.

difficulties.pattern: Using abbreviations from a previous hospital, country or textbook that are not used, or mean something different, locally.
difficulties.revealedBy: Abbreviations queried by assessors or ambiguous in the local context.
difficulties.response: Teach learners to check the approved abbreviation list for the placement and to expand any abbreviation that could be misread.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to order ten scrambled statements from a case presentation and to delete two that are not relevant to the presenting problem.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces the conventional order, deletes the irrelevant items and explains why.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Orders most items correctly but keeps irrelevant details or misplaces examination findings and history.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Orders the statements chronologically by when events happened, regardless of the conventional structure.

guidance.contextNotes: Medical students meet oral case presentations on clinical attachments from the early clinical years, and dental, pharmacy and allied-health students present cases in practice-based modules; support should be coordinated with clinical teaching. At PGT, practitioners present cases in advanced-practice and specialist modules, often with more critical engagement with evidence and service context. Conventions differ between specialties and countries, so learners who trained elsewhere may bring a different but valid order.
reviewNotes: The ID is kept for stability after care plans were split into their own topic (dhl.care-plans, R6-09); this topic now covers case presentations only.
Published clinical case reports in journals follow the CARE reporting guideline and are a research-publication genre not covered here; no CARE source is in the bibliography.

guidance.summary: Clinical communication is taught in health programmes through consultation models such as the Calgary–Cambridge guide described by Silverman et al. (2013), which set out structures for initiating, gathering information, explaining and planning, and closing. For multilingual students, the additional challenges are pragmatic (mitigating requests to senior staff, managing face with patients) and receptive (colloquial and regional speech). Politeness theory (Brown & Levinson, 1987) gives a vocabulary for discussing these choices, and Gigerenzer et al. (2007) show that how risk is framed affects patient understanding. Structured handover formats differ by service, so learners should check which is used on their placement.

activities.title: Lay explanation with explain-back
learnerActions: Prepare an explanation of a common procedure or condition for a patient with no medical knowledge
Deliver it in a role-play and ask the 'patient' to explain it back
Note where the explanation broke down and revise the wording, chunking information and replacing jargon
activities.intendedInsight: Checking understanding by asking the patient to explain back reveals misunderstandings that 'Do you understand?' hides.
activities.rationale: Explaining and checking understanding are core components of consultation models used in health education, and role-play allows safe rehearsal.

activities.title: Escalating to a senior colleague
learnerActions: Read a scenario in which a patient's condition is deteriorating
Plan a concise call to a senior colleague using the structured format used locally (situation, background, assessment, recommendation or similar)
Role-play the call and discuss how directness and politeness were balanced
activities.intendedInsight: In escalation, clarity and directness serve patient safety, and a structured format supports them.
activities.rationale: Politeness theory helps learners see that the degree of mitigation suitable in an academic request may be inappropriate when patient safety is at stake.

difficulties.pattern: Mitigating too much when raising concerns with senior staff ('I'm sorry to bother you, maybe if you have time…').
difficulties.revealedBy: Escalations in role-play or on placement where the concern and the request are unclear.
difficulties.response: Contrast the purposes of academic requests and clinical escalation, and practise a structured format that puts the concern first. Do not suggest that deference itself is wrong; show when the situation calls for directness.

difficulties.pattern: Not recognising colloquial or regional expressions for symptoms or body parts.
difficulties.revealedBy: Students who report that patients are hard to understand, or who misrecord symptoms.
difficulties.response: Build a class glossary from placement experiences, practise clarification questions, and use recordings of varied accents. Encourage asking rather than guessing.

difficulties.pattern: Using technical terms with patients because they are the precise terms learned in class.
difficulties.revealedBy: Role-plays in which patients look confused and the student does not notice.
difficulties.response: Practise translating terms into lay language and back. Make explain-back routine.

diagnostic.task: In a three-minute role-play, the learner must gather a brief history from a patient who uses one colloquial symptom description and then explain the next step.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses open then closed questions, clarifies the colloquial expression, acknowledges the patient's concern and checks understanding by asking for an explanation back.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gathers information but ignores the expression or relies on 'Do you understand?'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Asks only closed questions, uses jargon and does not check understanding.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional health pathways should introduce the basic interactional patterns before placements begin. UG students need support around first placements. International PGT practitioners may be clinically experienced but new to the communication norms and accents of the local health system.
reviewNotes: Clinical communication assessment (for example OSCE stations) is governed by professional programmes; EAP support should be coordinated with clinical skills staff.
Handover formats such as SBAR or ISBAR vary by service; no specific source is cited for them here.

guidance.summary: Appraisal tools structure the questions a reader asks about validity, results and applicability (Greenhalgh, 2019), but students often reproduce checklist answers rather than producing a judgement. Teaching should focus on turning appraisal findings into calibrated evaluative prose, on weighing weaknesses by their likely effect on the results, and on the vocabulary of bias and generalisability. Because evidence-based practice integrates research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values (Sackett et al., 1996), an appraisal should end with a judgement about applicability to a practice question, not only about the quality of the study.

activities.title: From checklist to judgement
learnerActions: Complete a design-appropriate appraisal checklist for a short study
Group the checklist answers into strengths and weaknesses and rank them by their likely effect on the results
Write a paragraph that gives an overall judgement and explains how the main weakness limits applicability
activities.intendedInsight: A checklist identifies issues; the written appraisal must weigh them and reach a conclusion.
activities.rationale: Structured appraisal is standard in health education, and converting it into weighed prose targets the evaluative step that markers reward.

activities.title: Weighing, not listing
learnerActions: Take a list of six limitations identified in a published study
Rank them by their likely effect on the direction or size of the result, and explain the top two
Write a concluding sentence on whether the findings should inform practice in a named setting
activities.intendedInsight: Appraisal weighs limitations by their consequences for the results and for practice.
activities.rationale: Linking appraisal to a practice decision reflects the evidence-based practice model, in which research evidence is one input into a judgement.

difficulties.pattern: Listing every limitation with equal weight, so that every study appears flawed.
difficulties.revealedBy: Appraisals that conclude a study is 'unreliable' without weighing the importance of each weakness.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to rank limitations by their likely effect and to state what the study can still support. Avoid praising long lists of weaknesses as criticality.

difficulties.pattern: Treating the appraisal tool's headings as the essay structure.
difficulties.revealedBy: Assignments organised as question-and-answer under checklist headings where an argued critique was required.
difficulties.response: Show exemplars of continuous appraisal writing and discuss how the brief signals the expected format.

diagnostic.task: Give a methods and results summary of a small study and ask for a 150-word appraisal paragraph ending with a recommendation about applicability.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the key validity issue, explains its likely effect, acknowledges strengths and gives a calibrated judgement about applying the findings.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies weaknesses but lists them without weighing, or concludes without linking to them.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the study without evaluation.

guidance.contextNotes: UG health students meet appraisal in research modules, often with one study and a prescribed tool. PGT students appraise several studies, often as the basis of literature-based dissertations, and need to weigh different designs against each other. PGR researchers revisit appraisal as risk-of-bias assessment within systematic and scoping reviews, covered by res.systematic-review-writing.
reviewNotes: The topic now covers appraisal of single studies; systematic and scoping review writing has moved to res.systematic-review-writing (R6-02). The recommended soft edge from this topic to res.systematic-review-writing belongs in the research-communication file, not here.
CASP, JBI and other appraisal tools are named as examples but not cited; tool choice varies by programme.

guidance.summary: Stylistics, as introduced by Short (1996), offers a systematic, linguistically grounded way into close reading: noticing foregrounding through deviation and parallelism, and connecting linguistic features to interpretation. This makes tacit literary-critical practice explicit, which benefits learners new to the discipline. Learners' own metalinguistic awareness from other languages can support the noticing stage. Because interpretation is valued over correct answers in humanities fields (Becher & Trowler, 2001), teaching should reward plausible, evidenced readings rather than a single meaning.

activities.title: Notice, then interpret
learnerActions: Read a short passage and list everything you notice about its language, without interpreting yet
Group your observations into patterns (repetitions, contrasts, shifts)
Choose one pattern and write a paragraph explaining what it contributes to meaning, quoting individual words
activities.intendedInsight: Interpretation is stronger when it grows from systematic noticing of patterns rather than from a general impression.
activities.rationale: Stylistic approaches make the observation-to-interpretation process explicit through foregrounding, deviation and parallelism.

activities.title: Two readings of one detail
learnerActions: Examine an ambiguous word or image in a passage
In pairs, develop two different interpretations, each supported by textual evidence
Write a paragraph that presents both and argues for one
activities.intendedInsight: Humanities interpretation is argued, not discovered, and alternatives strengthen an argument when addressed.
activities.rationale: Working with competing readings reflects the interpretive, plural character of knowledge in soft-pure disciplines.

difficulties.pattern: Retelling what happens in the passage instead of analysing how it is written.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that paraphrase plot or content, with feedback such as 'too much narrative' or 'analyse, don't describe'.
difficulties.response: Contrast summary and analysis using the same passage, and require each sentence to refer to a specific word or formal feature.

difficulties.pattern: Spotting devices and naming them ('This is a metaphor') without explaining their effect.
difficulties.revealedBy: Analyses that list techniques without linking them to meaning.
difficulties.response: Use a three-part frame (feature, effect, significance) and ask 'so what?' after each observation. Do not reward terminology for its own sake.

difficulties.pattern: There must be one correct interpretation, and I need to find what the teacher thinks.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to commit to an interpretation, or reliance on study guides.
difficulties.response: Discuss how interpretations are judged by evidence and plausibility, show published critics disagreeing, and value evidenced original readings.

diagnostic.task: Give a short poem or prose passage and ask for one analytical paragraph in 15 minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies a pattern, analyses specific words with brief quotations and connects features to an interpretation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names devices accurately but explains their effect only in general terms.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the content without analysis of language or form.

guidance.contextNotes: On foundation and pre-sessional humanities pathways, build the sequence from noticing to interpretation with short texts. UG students need support with depth and with using critical terminology. PGT students are expected to connect close reading with theory and critical debate.
reviewNotes: Close reading practices differ between literary studies, history and philosophy; examples here lean towards literary studies.

guidance.summary: Wineburg (1991) found that historians reading documents routinely used heuristics that novices did not: sourcing (attending to author and provenance), contextualisation and corroboration across documents. Coffin (2006) shows how student historical writing develops from recounting to explaining and arguing, which depends on treating sources as evidence to be interpreted rather than as records. Teaching should model these heuristics with authentic sources and make citation conventions for primary materials explicit, in consultation with the department and archivists.

activities.title: Source before content
learnerActions: Before reading a document's content, note its author, date, type, intended audience and purpose
Predict how these might shape what it says
Read the document and write two sentences on what it can and cannot reliably tell you about a stated question
activities.intendedInsight: The value of a source depends on who produced it and why, in relation to the question asked.
activities.rationale: Sourcing is a heuristic Wineburg observed in historians but not in novices, so modelling it targets a key difference in expertise.

activities.title: Corroboration table
learnerActions: Read three short sources on the same event
Tabulate where they agree, disagree and are silent
Write a paragraph explaining the discrepancies with reference to each source's origin and purpose
activities.intendedInsight: Discrepancies between sources are themselves evidence about perspective and context.
activities.rationale: Corroboration and explanation of difference move student writing from recount towards historical argument.

difficulties.pattern: Treating a document as a neutral record of what happened.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays that quote primary sources as fact without considering authorship or purpose.
difficulties.response: Make sourcing a routine first step and ask for a reliability comment whenever a primary source is used.

difficulties.pattern: Not knowing how to cite archives, manuscripts or translated sources.
difficulties.revealedBy: Incomplete or inconsistent citations for primary materials, missing repository or translation details.
difficulties.response: Provide models in the required style and liaise with the department and library on local expectations.

diagnostic.task: Give a primary source with a clear author and purpose and ask the learner to write a short commentary on its usefulness for a stated question.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Sources and contextualises the document, notes what it reveals and what it obscures, and suggests what other sources would corroborate it.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Summarises content and mentions the author but does not link authorship to reliability.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats the document as factual narrative.

guidance.contextNotes: UG history and related students meet primary sources in seminars and coursework. PGT dissertations often involve archival work for the first time. PGR researchers need detailed control of archival citation, transcription and translation conventions and of research ethics for archives.
reviewNotes: Wineburg's study compared historians with high-school students; the heuristics are widely applied in university teaching but the study did not test university learners.

guidance.summary: Coffin (2006) describes a developmental path in historical writing from recount genres, through explanation, to argument genres (exposition, discussion and challenge), in which evaluation and engagement with other views become central. Martin and White's (2005) engagement system gives a vocabulary for how writers position their interpretations among others, and Hyland (2004) shows that humanities and social science writers use more explicit evaluation of sources and authorial presence than scientists. Teaching should help learners formulate arguable interpretive theses, build paragraphs around claims, and position themselves in the critical conversation.

activities.title: Is it arguable?
learnerActions: Sort a set of thesis statements into summary, fact and interpretation
Rewrite the summary and fact statements as interpretive claims
Test each claim by writing the opposing claim and judging whether a reasonable reader could hold it
activities.intendedInsight: An interpretive thesis is a claim that could be disputed and must be argued.
activities.rationale: Distinguishing recount and record from argument targets the developmental shift Coffin identifies in historical and other humanities writing.

activities.title: Entering the critical conversation
learnerActions: Read two short critical views on a text or historical question
Highlight the language each writer uses to agree, concede, counter or extend
Write a paragraph positioning your interpretation in relation to both critics
activities.intendedInsight: Interpretation is made persuasive by engaging other readings explicitly.
activities.rationale: The engagement system describes how writers open and close dialogic space, giving learners concrete resources for positioning.

difficulties.pattern: Writing a thesis that summarises the text or restates a fact.
difficulties.revealedBy: Introductions with descriptive theses and essays that follow the order of the text.
difficulties.response: Practise converting summaries into claims and organising paragraphs by argument rather than by chronology of the text.

difficulties.pattern: In my previous studies marks came from reproducing the accepted reading, so I summarise critics rather than taking a position on them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays that report critics' views approvingly without positioning the writer's own reading.
difficulties.response: Model respectful disagreement and extension, and show exemplars in which students challenge or refine critics. Present this as a disciplinary expectation shaped by assessment criteria, not as a rejection of respect for scholarship.

difficulties.pattern: Using long quotations that substitute for analysis.
difficulties.revealedBy: Block quotations followed by brief comment.
difficulties.response: Require short, embedded quotations and analysis that is longer than the quotation.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write an interpretive thesis and one supporting paragraph on a short set text or source.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Arguable thesis, claim-led paragraph with brief analysed quotations, reference to an alternative reading.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Interpretive thesis but paragraph drifts into summary or uses quotation without analysis.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Descriptive thesis and summary paragraph.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional humanities pathways, focus on the move from summary to interpretation. UG students need support with claim-led paragraphs and quotation. PGT and PGR writers must position original interpretations within critical or historiographical debates over long texts.
reviewNotes: Conventions differ markedly between literary studies, history and other humanities fields; exemplars should come from the learner's discipline.

guidance.summary: Philosophy essays are organised around reconstructing and assessing arguments, and Walton (2006) provides tools for identifying argument structure and the critical questions that test it. Hyland (2001, 2004) found that writers in philosophy and other soft fields use self-mention far more than those in the sciences, which supports teaching first-person signposting as a disciplinary convention rather than discouraging it. Teaching should emphasise charitable reconstruction, targeted objections and clear distinctions, and should use departmental guidance and model essays.

activities.title: Standard form
learnerActions: Read a short passage presenting a philosophical argument
Rewrite it as numbered premises and a conclusion, adding any unstated premise needed for validity
Compare reconstructions with a partner and decide which is more faithful and charitable
activities.intendedInsight: Reconstruction is an interpretive act that should present the argument at its strongest.
activities.rationale: Identifying premises, conclusions and implicit assumptions is central to argument analysis as Walton describes it.

activities.title: Objection and reply
learnerActions: Choose one premise from a reconstructed argument
Write an objection using a counterexample or thought experiment
Write the strongest reply the original author could give, then a paragraph assessing whether the reply succeeds, using first-person signposting
activities.intendedInsight: Philosophical argument progresses through targeted objections and replies, with the writer's moves made explicit.
activities.rationale: Objection–reply practice reflects the dialectical structure of philosophy essays, and first-person signposting is a documented feature of philosophical writing.

difficulties.pattern: Summarising what philosophers said, in historical order, without evaluating the arguments.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays that resemble history-of-ideas surveys with little argument assessment.
