difficulties.response: Show model essays where exposition serves evaluation, and limit exposition to what the argument needs.

difficulties.pattern: Objecting to a conclusion because I disagree with it, without identifying which premise fails.
difficulties.revealedBy: Objections that state an opposing view rather than targeting the argument's structure.
difficulties.response: Teach validity and soundness explicitly and require every objection to name the premise or inference it targets.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding 'I' because I was taught it is not academic.
difficulties.revealedBy: Convoluted impersonal constructions where a philosopher would write 'I will argue'.
difficulties.response: Show evidence of self-mention in philosophy and the department's guidance. Present 'never use I' as a myth, while noting that conventions vary.

diagnostic.task: Give a short argumentative passage and ask the learner to reconstruct it in standard form and raise one objection.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Faithful, valid reconstruction with any implicit premise made explicit, and an objection targeting a specific premise with a counterexample.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reasonable reconstruction but the objection is a general disagreement.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summary of the passage without premise–conclusion structure.

guidance.contextNotes: UG philosophy students meet these conventions from the first year, often with departmental style guides. PGT students may come from other disciplines and need explicit induction. PGR researchers need to sustain argument across long texts with careful signposting.
reviewNotes: Philosophical writing conventions differ between analytic and continental traditions; this topic reflects mainly analytic practice common in UK departments.

guidance.summary: Bhatia (1993) shows that features often criticised as obscure in legal English, such as complex qualifications in legislative sentences, serve the drafter's aim of precision and all-inclusiveness. Mertz (2007) describes legal education as a linguistic reorientation in which students learn to read texts for legal categories and authority rather than for moral or narrative meaning. Teaching should therefore explain the functions of legal features, distinguish what learners need to recognise from what they should produce, and emphasise that legal terms belong to a specific legal system.

activities.title: Same word, different law
learnerActions: Collect five words from a case you are reading that have both everyday and legal meanings
Write the everyday meaning and the legal meaning side by side, using a legal dictionary to check
Write one sentence in your own words using each word in its legal sense
activities.intendedInsight: Many difficult legal words look familiar, and the familiar meaning can lead to a wrong reading.
activities.rationale: Reading for legal rather than everyday meaning is the reorientation Mertz describes as central to legal education.

activities.title: Why is it written like this?
learnerActions: Read a short statutory provision and a plain-language version of it
Identify what the original says that the plain version leaves out or makes less precise
Discuss which features of the original you should recognise when reading and which you should avoid in your own analytical writing
activities.intendedInsight: Legal drafting features serve precision and inclusiveness, but student analysis is expected to be clear rather than imitative.
activities.rationale: Bhatia's analysis of legislative writing shows how its complexity follows from its purpose, which helps learners read it without imitating it.

difficulties.pattern: Translating legal terms through a bilingual dictionary or assuming they mean what the closest term means in the legal system I studied.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misuse of concepts such as consideration, equity or trust, which have no direct equivalent in many civil-law systems.
difficulties.response: Treat legal terms as system-specific concepts. Use an English legal dictionary and the cases that define them, and note differences from the learner's home legal system as a comparative resource.

difficulties.pattern: Imitating archaic drafting in my essays (hereinafter, the said party, aforementioned) because it sounds legal.
difficulties.revealedBy: Student essays and problem answers with drafting formulas that markers mark as unclear or inappropriate.
difficulties.response: Distinguish reading legal drafting from writing legal analysis, and show model answers in clear academic prose.

diagnostic.task: Give six sentences from judgments and statutes, each with a highlighted word, and ask the learner to explain the meaning of each in context.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives the legal meaning for all items and explains how the everyday sense would mislead for at least two.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Recognises some legal senses but defaults to everyday meanings for less familiar words.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives everyday meanings throughout.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional law pathways, focus on recognition and on frequently confused legal senses. UG students need terminology tied to core modules. LLM students often know legal concepts in their own system well, so comparative discussion is valuable, alongside explicit warning about false equivalents.
reviewNotes: The topic assumes common-law, primarily English, legal English; programmes in other jurisdictions should adapt examples.

guidance.summary: Bhatia (1993) describes legal cases as a genre with recognisable moves (identifying the case, establishing the facts, arguing the case, pronouncing judgment), which gives learners a map for reading. Twining and Miers (2010) treat reading cases and extracting the ratio as an interpretive skill, noting that the ratio is not stated in the judgment and that its formulation can be contested. Mertz (2007) shows that law students learn to read cases for legal authority and procedure rather than for the human story. Teaching should model the process of briefing, practise it with real judgments, and discuss competing formulations of the ratio.

activities.title: Map the judgment
learnerActions: Skim a short judgment and mark where the facts, procedural history, arguments, reasoning and decision appear
Highlight the sentences that state the legal principle the decision depends on
Compare the headnote with your reading and note anything the headnote simplifies
activities.intendedInsight: Judgments have a recognisable structure, and the headnote is a guide to them, not a substitute.
activities.rationale: Genre awareness of the moves in a legal case supports strategic reading of long judgments.

activities.title: How wide is the ratio?
learnerActions: Write the ratio of a case in one sentence
Compare formulations across the group, from very narrow (tied to the exact facts) to very broad
Discuss which formulation the material facts justify, and identify one obiter statement and why it is not binding
activities.intendedInsight: Formulating the ratio is an interpretive act, and its level of generality matters for later cases.
activities.rationale: Twining and Miers present the ratio as something readers construct from the judgment, which group comparison makes visible.

difficulties.pattern: Reading the judgment from start to finish and summarising everything, or relying only on the headnote.
difficulties.revealedBy: Case briefs that retell the facts at length, or that reproduce headnote wording without the reasoning.
difficulties.response: Teach strategic reading with the case structure and set a strict length for briefs. Explain that the headnote is not authority.

difficulties.pattern: Treating everything a senior judge says as binding law.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays and problem answers that cite obiter remarks as if they were the ratio, or dissenting judgments as authority.
difficulties.response: Practise separating ratio, obiter and dissent, and explain precedential weight with the court hierarchy.

diagnostic.task: Give a 500-word extract from a judgment and ask the learner to identify the issue, the decision, the ratio in one sentence and any obiter remark.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the issue as a legal question, formulates a ratio grounded in material facts and correctly identifies obiter remarks.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies issue and decision but gives a ratio that restates the outcome or confuses it with obiter.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the facts without identifying the legal principle.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional law pathways, use short, accessible judgments; UG entrants need the basic structure of a judgment, while LLM entrants need explicit work on precedent. First-year LLB students need briefing practice early, coordinated with their legal method modules. LLM students from civil-law systems may be used to codes and academic doctrine as primary sources and need explicit work on precedent and on extracting the ratio.
reviewNotes: Mertz's study concerns US law schools; its relevance to UK legal education is by analogy.

The four-move description of judgments follows Bhatia's (1993) analysis of legal cases; judgments of some courts and jurisdictions do not follow it closely, so it is offered as a reading map rather than a fixed structure.

guidance.summary: Problem questions test the application of legal rules to facts, which Twining and Miers (2010) treat as a core interpretive skill of legal method. Scaffolds such as IRAC help novices organise answers, but they are contested: lecturers vary in whether they recommend them, and applied mechanically they lead to rule-stating with little application. Teaching should use IRAC-type structures as a starting point, foreground application to facts and the handling of ambiguity, and follow the conventions of the specific law school, including OSCOLA footnoting (Goudkamp, 2026).

activities.title: Issue spotting
learnerActions: Read a problem scenario and underline every fact that may have legal significance
Group the facts into legal issues and decide the order in which to address them
Compare your list with a lecturer's model issue list and discuss any issues you missed
activities.intendedInsight: Each significant fact is usually there for a reason, and missing an issue costs more than imperfect expression.
activities.rationale: Issue identification is the first step of applying rules to facts and a common source of lost marks.

activities.title: Apply, don't recite
learnerActions: Read two answers to the same issue: one that states the law at length and one that applies it closely to the facts
Highlight sentences that mention the specific facts of the scenario
Rewrite a rule-heavy paragraph so that at least half of it applies the rule to the facts, using analogy with or distinction from a decided case
activities.intendedInsight: Marks are earned mainly in application: connecting the rule to these facts through comparison with decided cases.
activities.rationale: Comparing answers makes the balance between rule statement and application visible, addressing a known weakness of mechanical IRAC use.

difficulties.pattern: Writing everything I know about the area of law and then giving a one-line conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that resemble essays on the topic, with little reference to the parties or facts.
difficulties.response: Show the marking criteria for application and require each paragraph to mention a fact from the scenario. Avoid presenting IRAC as a formula to fill.

difficulties.pattern: Giving certain conclusions ('X will definitely win') or refusing to conclude because the law is uncertain.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions that overstate certainty or leave the client without advice.
difficulties.response: Teach language for calibrated advice (is likely to, has a strong argument that, may be able to) and show how lawyers advise despite uncertainty.

difficulties.pattern: Inventing facts to resolve ambiguity in the scenario.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that assume facts not stated, such as what a party intended.
difficulties.response: Model conditional analysis that addresses each possibility (if X intended…, if, however,…). Explain that examiners include ambiguity on purpose.

diagnostic.task: Give a short problem scenario raising one main issue and one ambiguous fact, and ask for a 250-word answer advising one party.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the issue, gives the rule with authority, applies it closely with an analogy or distinction, addresses the ambiguous fact conditionally and concludes with calibrated advice.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the issue and rule correctly but applies them thinly or ignores the ambiguity.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Discusses the area of law generally without applying it or advising the party.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional law pathways, introduce the genre with short scenarios. First-year LLB students need support as they meet problem questions in exams and coursework. LLM students may not have met problem questions in their prior legal education, which often used other assessment forms.
reviewNotes: Critiques of IRAC are widespread among legal educators but are not documented by a source in the bibliography; they are presented here as a matter of practitioner debate.
Some UK law schools discourage IRAC labels and others teach them explicitly; check local practice.

guidance.summary: Bhatia (1993) analyses legislative provisions as sentences in which qualifications are inserted at points of potential ambiguity to make the provision precise and all-inclusive, which explains much of their reading difficulty. Twining and Miers (2010) treat statutory interpretation as reasoning about rules and their purposes, not only as the parsing of text. Teaching should combine structural parsing (main rule, conditions, exceptions, definitions) with awareness of how courts approach interpretation.

activities.title: Statute to flowchart
learnerActions: Read a statutory subsection and identify the main rule
Mark each condition, exception and cross-reference
Draw a flowchart or decision tree showing when the rule applies, then test it against two short fact scenarios
activities.intendedInsight: A long provision becomes manageable when its rule, conditions and exceptions are separated.
activities.rationale: Bhatia's account of qualificational insertion explains where the complexity lies, and visualising the structure supports accurate reading.

activities.title: Same words, different readings
learnerActions: Read a short provision with a known interpretive problem
In groups, argue for a literal reading and for a purposive reading
Write one paragraph explaining which reading you prefer and why, referring to the purpose of the Act
activities.intendedInsight: Reading legislation involves interpretive choices that courts justify by reference to the text and its purpose.
activities.rationale: Treating interpretation as reasoning about rules follows Twining and Miers' approach to statutory interpretation.

difficulties.pattern: Reading 'and' and 'or' between conditions loosely, so that cumulative conditions become alternatives or vice versa.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that apply a provision when only one of several cumulative conditions is met.
difficulties.response: Practise marking conjunctions in provisions and converting them into lists and flowcharts. Slow, structural reading is expected here.

difficulties.pattern: Ignoring the definitions section and reading defined terms in their ordinary sense.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misapplication of provisions in which a term has a specific statutory meaning.
difficulties.response: Make checking the interpretation section a routine step and show cases where a definition changed the outcome.

diagnostic.task: Give a 70-word statutory provision with two cumulative conditions and an exception, plus two short scenarios. Ask whether the provision applies in each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Applies the provision correctly to both scenarios and explains the conditions and the exception.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the main rule but misreads a condition or the exception.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Answers from general fairness without reference to the provision's structure.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional law pathways, use short provisions to build structural reading. UG students meet statutes in public, criminal and contract law. LLM students need efficient navigation of long Acts and secondary legislation, and may compare common-law statutory interpretation with civil-law code interpretation.

guidance.summary: Legal essays combine accurate exposition of the law with argument about it, and students often over-describe cases at the expense of evaluation. Mertz (2007) shows that legal reading attends to the authority and procedural position of texts, which in essays becomes a hierarchy of sources and reporting verbs with legal meanings. OSCOLA (Goudkamp, 2026) specifies footnote referencing for UK law schools. Teaching should use the school's exemplars, model how case discussion is subordinated to a thesis, and make legal reporting conventions explicit.

activities.title: From case list to argument
learnerActions: Read a paragraph that summarises three cases in turn
Decide what claim the three cases could support together
Rewrite the paragraph with the claim first and each case used as evidence, with OSCOLA footnotes
activities.intendedInsight: Cases are evidence for an argument about the law, not the content of the essay in themselves.
activities.rationale: Reordering source-by-source paragraphs into claim-led ones targets the most common weakness in legal essays.

activities.title: Who said what, with what authority?
learnerActions: Collect reporting verbs from a model essay and sort them by who they report (court, judge, counsel, commentator, Law Commission)
Discuss why 'held' is reserved for the court's decision and what 'observed' or 'suggested' signals
Correct the reporting verbs in a short student paragraph
activities.intendedInsight: In legal writing, reporting verbs signal legal authority as well as stance.
activities.rationale: Making legal reporting conventions explicit connects general reporting-verb knowledge to the authority structure Mertz describes.

difficulties.pattern: Describing the facts of every case at length.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays in which case narratives dominate, with feedback such as 'too descriptive' or 'what is your argument?'.
difficulties.response: Limit facts to those needed for the point and require a claim sentence at the start of each paragraph. Do not ban case facts; select them.

difficulties.pattern: Citing textbooks for propositions of law instead of the primary authority.
difficulties.revealedBy: Footnotes to textbooks where the marker expects a case or statute.
difficulties.response: Explain the hierarchy of authority and the role of secondary sources in legal argument, and practise tracing a textbook statement to its primary source.

diagnostic.task: Give a 'To what extent…' legal essay question and ask the learner for a thesis statement and one body paragraph with footnotes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Takes a clear position, uses cases as evidence for a claim, evaluates against a criterion and footnotes correctly in OSCOLA.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a position but the paragraph describes cases with little evaluation, or references are inconsistent.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the law without a position and without legal referencing.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional law pathways, contrast legal essays with general argumentative essays. UG students need early support with OSCOLA and with using cases as evidence. LLM essays expect more theoretical and comparative depth, and LLM students may bring different conventions for referencing and for the role of academic doctrine.
reviewNotes: Some institutions use OSCOLA variants or other legal citation guides; check local requirements.

guidance.summary: Halliday's analysis in Halliday and Martin (1993) treats the features that make scientific English hard (interlocking definitions, technical taxonomies, lexical density, grammatical metaphor) as functional resources that evolved to build and argue about technical knowledge. Teaching therefore aims at making these resources visible and usable, not at simplifying them away: learners practise unpacking nominalised sentences into congruent clauses and repacking them, and map the taxonomies that terms belong to. Lemke (1990) adds that science is learned by talking and writing its semantic relations, so learners should rehearse the relations between terms, not only the terms.

activities.title: Unpack and repack
learnerActions: Take a dense sentence from a course textbook and underline every noun that names a process or quality
Rewrite the sentence as a series of short clauses with human or physical agents and verbs
Compare versions with a partner and decide what the original version gains (flow from the previous sentence, compactness, a nameable concept) and what it loses (agency, explicit causal relation)
Repack a different explained sequence into one sentence using a process noun as the subject
activities.intendedInsight: Nominalisation lets science turn a process into a thing that can be measured, classified and used as the starting point of the next claim, at the cost of hiding who did what.
activities.rationale: Halliday's account of grammatical metaphor explains both the function and the reading difficulty of nominalised scientific prose, and moving between congruent and metaphorical wordings makes the resource visible.

activities.title: Taxonomy mapping
learnerActions: List the technical terms introduced in one section of a textbook chapter
Arrange them in a diagram showing classification (types of) and composition (parts of) relations
Write two definition sentences that use the diagram's superordinate terms (for example a covalent bond is a type of chemical bond in which…)
Check the diagram against a glossary or a subject lecturer's explanation
activities.intendedInsight: Scientific terms are organised into systems, and knowing a term includes knowing its place in the system.
activities.rationale: Halliday and Martin and Lemke both describe technical taxonomies as central to how science organises meaning, and making them explicit gives learners a structure for vocabulary learning.

difficulties.pattern: Scientific texts are hard just because the vocabulary is difficult. If I learn the words I will understand.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners who can gloss every word in a sentence still misread which process caused which, or cannot say what a nominalised subject refers back to.
difficulties.response: Show that difficulty often lies in grammar: process nouns, long nominal groups and implicit causal links. Practise unpacking. Do not simply pre-teach word lists and assume comprehension follows.

difficulties.pattern: Using everyday meanings of words that are technical in the discipline (writing that a force 'has power' or a result is 'significant' meaning important).
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that are grammatical but scientifically wrong, often flagged by subject markers as conceptual errors.
difficulties.response: Contrast everyday and technical uses side by side and ask learners to collect pairs from their own reading. Involve subject staff in checking which distinctions matter most in the module.

difficulties.pattern: Packing every sentence with nominalisations to sound scientific, producing writing that hides agents and causal steps.
difficulties.revealedBy: Student drafts with strings of abstract nouns that markers comment on as unclear or wordy.
difficulties.response: Present nominalisation as a choice with costs. Ask learners to justify each nominalisation by what it does for text flow and to unpack those that do nothing. Avoid presenting density as a target in itself.

diagnostic.task: Give a 40–60-word textbook extract with two nominalisations and one sub-technical term. Ask the learner to explain it orally in plain terms and then identify which word has a special scientific meaning.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Recovers the underlying processes and agents, keeps the causal direction, and identifies the sub-technical term and its scientific sense.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Paraphrases the general topic but blurs the causal relation or replaces a technical term with an everyday synonym.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Translates word by word or restates the sentence unchanged, unable to say what happens to what.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation, work from textbooks and practical classes, with a strong focus on taxonomies and on unpacking dense sentences. On pre-sessional science pathways, use subject texts to build awareness of the register; PG entrants should work with research prose from their field. In-sessionally, connect the work to the student’s module reading and to markers’ comments about clarity. At PGT, the topic is mainly revisited when discussing when compressed prose helps research writing and when it becomes unreadable.

guidance.summary: Sydney School genre research distinguishes several explanation genres (sequential, causal, factorial, consequential, conditional) with predictable stages: identifying the phenomenon, then an explanation sequence (Martin & Rose, 2008). Explicit teaching of these stages through deconstruction, joint construction and independent construction is a central proposal of the Reading to Learn pedagogy (Rose & Martin, 2012). Gardner and Nesi (2013) also identify Explanation as a distinct genre family in university student writing, particularly in science and technology disciplines.

activities.title: Which kind of explanation?
learnerActions: Sort six short textbook explanations into sequential, factorial and consequential types
Highlight the identifying statement and the language that links each step or factor
Choose an explanation type for each of three exam questions from your subject and justify the choice
activities.intendedInsight: The question asked determines the shape of the explanation, and each shape has its own linking language.
activities.rationale: Identifying the staging and purpose of explanation genres before writing them follows the deconstruction phase of the Sydney School teaching–learning cycle.

activities.title: Joint construction with a diagram
learnerActions: Start from a labelled diagram of a process from your module, such as a cycle or a circuit
Build an explanation together with the teacher, deciding the order of steps and the causal verb for each link
Write a second explanation independently from a different diagram and compare it with a model
activities.intendedInsight: Diagrams show stages but not reasons; the written explanation must add the causal links.
activities.rationale: Joint construction scaffolds the move from understanding a model text to producing one, and diagram-to-text work reflects how science presents explanations multimodally.

difficulties.pattern: Narrating what happened in one experiment ('First we heated the water, then…') when the question asks for a general explanation of a mechanism.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers in past tense with personal agents and specific quantities, where the marker expected present-tense general statements.
difficulties.response: Contrast a recount of a practical with an explanation of the phenomenon it demonstrates. Show the shift to present simple and to generic participants.

difficulties.pattern: Listing steps or factors joined by 'and' or 'then' without saying how one causes the next.
difficulties.revealedBy: Explanations that read as sequences of true statements but lose marks for 'no explanation of why'.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to label each link with the causal relation (causes, enables, prevents) and to choose a verb or conjunction for it. Do not correct only surface linking words; check the logic of each step with subject knowledge.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain a familiar phenomenon from their subject in writing in about 120 words, with an optional sketch.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the phenomenon, then orders the steps or factors, links each causally, uses technical terms accurately and stays general.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Covers the right content but with weak or missing causal links, or slips into a recount of a particular case.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the topic or gives a definition without any explanation sequence.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional pathways for UG science entrants, this is a core genre for exams and short answers and can be taught with textbook and practical-class material. In UG in-sessional work, link it to exam answers and to the discussion sections of lab reports, where theoretical explanation of results is expected.
reviewNotes: The theoretical explanation type in the scope note is not a separate Sydney School category; it is interpreted here as applying a model or law to a specific case.

guidance.summary: Procedural and specification texts are judged by whether they can be carried out or tested without ambiguity, so teaching should focus on precision, sequencing and the conventional meanings of modal verbs in the relevant community. Trimble (1985) describes instructions and rhetorical functions such as description of process and of physical structure as central to scientific and technical English. Gardner and Nesi (2013) identify Design Specification as a genre family in student writing. Conventions for modal verbs and formatting vary across standards bodies, companies and departments, so learners should check the local standard or template with subject staff.

activities.title: Follow it exactly
learnerActions: Write a protocol for a simple procedure (for example preparing a 0.1 M solution or setting up a piece of software)
Exchange protocols with a partner, who follows the steps literally and records every point where they had to guess
Revise the protocol to remove each guess, adding quantities, conditions, timings or warnings
activities.intendedInsight: A protocol is only as good as the questions it leaves unanswered for the person following it.
activities.rationale: Literal execution makes ambiguity visible to the writer, a form of reader feedback that matches the genre's purpose.

activities.title: Testable requirements
learnerActions: Read a short design brief and underline every vague expression (fast, user-friendly, approximately)
Rewrite each as a single requirement with a measurable criterion and unit
Assign each requirement a modal verb according to the convention your department or the relevant standard uses, and justify the choice
activities.intendedInsight: Specification language turns intentions into statements that can be passed or failed.
activities.rationale: Converting vague briefs into verifiable statements targets the core function of the design specification genre and the precise use of units and quantities.

difficulties.pattern: Writing protocols in the past passive ('The solution was heated') because that is how lab-report methods are written.
difficulties.revealedBy: Protocols or SOPs that read as reports of what was done rather than instructions to follow.
difficulties.response: Place a protocol and the corresponding lab-report method side by side and discuss how purpose and reader change mood, tense and voice.

difficulties.pattern: Using should, must and will interchangeably in requirements, or using 'shall' and 'should' in their everyday senses.
difficulties.revealedBy: Specifications in which the obligation level of each requirement is unclear; this is more likely where the writer’s other languages mark degrees of obligation with different or fewer distinctions.
difficulties.response: Teach the convention used by the relevant standard or department explicitly as a convention, and have learners audit their own specifications for consistency.

difficulties.pattern: Omitting units, conditions or tolerances because they seem obvious to the writer.
difficulties.revealedBy: Quantities without units, temperatures without duration, or settings without the equipment model.
difficulties.response: Use a checklist for quantity, unit, condition, duration and equipment for each step. Peer testing is more effective than teacher correction alone here.

diagnostic.task: Give a five-step protocol containing one missing unit, one warning placed after the hazardous step and one step that combines two actions. Ask the learner to edit it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Fixes all three problems and explains how each would affect a person following the protocol.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices the missing unit but not the misplaced warning or the compound step.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Edits only grammar or style and leaves the procedural problems untouched.

guidance.contextNotes: UG science and engineering students read protocols in practical classes and write specifications in design projects; start from reading instructions accurately and move to writing verifiable requirements. PGT engineering and computing students write specifications in group and individual projects. PGR researchers may write standard operating procedures, method statements or protocols for ethics and safety approval, where institutional templates apply.
reviewNotes: The modal-verb convention (shall/must for mandatory, should for recommended, may for optional) varies between standards bodies and organisations; it is presented as a convention to check locally, not as a universal rule.

guidance.summary: Experimental vocabulary is a site where language and conceptual understanding are inseparable: confusion between accuracy and precision, or between significance and importance, often signals a misunderstanding of method. Parkinson's (2017) analysis of the student laboratory report shows how aims, methods and discussions rest on this vocabulary, and Hyland's (1998) work on scientific hedging shows that expert writers tie certainty to the strength of experimental evidence. Teaching should pair language work with simple experimental scenarios and, where possible, with lab demonstrators' feedback.

activities.title: Variable detective
learnerActions: Read three short experiment descriptions from your subject
Identify the independent, dependent and controlled variables and the control condition in each
Write a hypothesis and a prediction for each, and compare formulations with a partner
activities.intendedInsight: A hypothesis states a relationship between named variables, and a prediction says what should be observed if it holds.
activities.rationale: Working from authentic experimental designs ties the vocabulary to the concepts it encodes, as in the aims and methods stages of student lab reports.

activities.title: Error and uncertainty clinic
learnerActions: Examine sets of repeated measurements that are precise but inaccurate, accurate but imprecise, and both
Label each set and write one sentence describing it with appropriate vocabulary
Rewrite three overclaiming result statements so that they state the value with its uncertainty and make a claim the data can support
activities.intendedInsight: Accuracy, precision and uncertainty are different properties, and claims should not exceed what the measurements show.
activities.rationale: Connecting the language of uncertainty to claim strength reflects how scientific writers calibrate certainty to evidence, and to statistical guidance against equating significance with importance.

difficulties.pattern: Using 'error' to mean a mistake by the experimenter, and listing 'human error' as the main limitation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussion sections that blame 'human error' without naming a source of random or systematic error or its effect on the result.
difficulties.response: Teach the scientific sense of error as uncertainty, and ask learners to name a specific source, classify it and suggest how it could be reduced. Agree with lab staff what level of error analysis is expected.

difficulties.pattern: Writing hypotheses as questions or as vague expectations ('Temperature will affect the reaction').
difficulties.revealedBy: Hypotheses that do not state the direction or nature of the relationship and so cannot be tested.
difficulties.response: Model the move from question to directional hypothesis to measurable prediction. Note that some fields and some lab reports do not require formal hypotheses, so check the brief.

diagnostic.task: Give a results table from a simple experiment, with repeats, and ask the learner to write two sentences: one reporting the result with uncertainty, one evaluating the reliability of the data.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Reports a mean with an appropriate uncertainty and significant figures, and evaluates spread and possible systematic error using the correct terms.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reports the mean but without uncertainty, or uses accuracy and precision interchangeably.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Copies values without interpretation or attributes all variation to 'human error'.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional science pathways, link this to practical classes and simple data. In UG in-sessional work, align it with lab reports and demonstrator feedback. At PGT the focus shifts to statistical language and uncertainty in project work, where num.interpreting-statistics becomes more relevant.

guidance.summary: Software documentation is a family of genres defined by readers with different tasks: a newcomer deciding whether to use a project, a developer calling an API, a maintainer reading code months later. Robillard's (2009) survey of developers found inadequate documentation, especially missing examples and explanations of intent, to be a major obstacle to learning APIs, which supports teaching documentation around reader tasks rather than templates. Conventions differ between languages, frameworks and teams, so learners should analyse documentation from well-maintained projects in their own ecosystem and check module requirements.

activities.title: README rescue
learnerActions: Compare two READMEs from open-source projects in your language, one that you find easy to use and one that you do not
List the sections each contains and what questions a newcomer can or cannot answer from each
Rewrite the README of one of your own projects so that a classmate can install and run it, then test it with that classmate
activities.intendedInsight: A README is judged by whether a newcomer can get started without asking the author.
activities.rationale: Analysing authentic exemplars and then testing with a real reader applies genre analysis to a professional genre whose success criteria are practical.

activities.title: Why, not what
learnerActions: Read a short code file with a mix of comments
Classify each comment as restating the code, explaining intent, warning of a constraint or out of date
Rewrite or delete comments accordingly and write one docstring with parameters, return value, errors and an example
activities.intendedInsight: Good comments carry information the code cannot express, such as purpose and reasons for a non-obvious choice.
activities.rationale: Developers report that documentation explaining intent and usage is what they most often lack, so classifying comments by function directs attention to that information.

difficulties.pattern: The code is the documentation. If it works, that is enough.
difficulties.revealedBy: Projects submitted with no README or only auto-generated stubs, and marks lost on maintainability criteria.
difficulties.response: Show the marking criteria and a maintainer's task that cannot be done from the code alone. Bring in a subject tutor's or developer's view of documentation as part of the product.

difficulties.pattern: Writing comments that translate each line into English (increment i by 1).
difficulties.revealedBy: High comment density with no information about intent, constraints or reasons.
difficulties.response: Have learners delete every comment that a competent reader could reconstruct from the code, then add one explaining why for each non-obvious block. Do not reward comment quantity.

difficulties.pattern: Using informal, inconsistent wording across documentation, mixing imperative and descriptive styles for instructions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Installation steps that switch between 'You need to…', 'Run…' and 'The user should…', and parameter descriptions in different formats.
difficulties.response: Agree a style for the project, such as imperative steps and a fixed docstring format, and use a checklist or linter where the ecosystem provides one.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write the opening of a README (purpose sentence, prerequisites, one usage example) for a small program they have written.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States what the program does and for whom in one sentence, lists prerequisites with versions, and gives a runnable example with expected output.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Includes a purpose and example but omits prerequisites, or describes features instead of showing usage.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writes a narrative of how the program was developed rather than how to use it.

guidance.contextNotes: For UG computing students, focus on README, comments and docstrings in assessed projects. At PGT, add design documents and API documentation for group projects. For PGR researchers, emphasise documentation of research software and code for reproducibility and data sharing.
reviewNotes: Research on documentation in EAP is sparse; guidance draws on software-engineering research on developer needs and on genre analysis, and should be reviewed with computing staff.

guidance.summary: Mathematical writing combines symbolic notation with English that carries the logic: quantifiers, conditionals and inference markers. Style guides for the mathematical sciences such as Higham (1998) give conventions for integrating notation into sentences, defining symbols and signalling proof structure. Gardner and Nesi (2013) classify mathematical problem solutions within the Exercise genre family, in which demonstrating reasoning is the assessed purpose. Many learners arrive from systems that assessed final answers, so the expectation of written justification should be made explicit with lecturers' exemplars.

activities.title: From calculation to proof
learnerActions: Compare an answer-only solution and a full written proof of the same result
Highlight the words in the proof that do logical work (let, suppose, hence, since, therefore)
Rewrite a second answer-only solution as a proof, then compare with a lecturer's model
activities.intendedInsight: In a proof, the words between the equations are where the reasoning is shown and assessed.
activities.rationale: Making the logical vocabulary of proofs visible and practising conversion targets the specific conventions that mathematical style guides describe.

activities.title: Read it aloud
learnerActions: Read a written proof aloud, including the symbols, as full sentences
Mark every place where the result is not a grammatical sentence or where a symbol appears without having been introduced
Revise your own proof until it reads aloud as continuous prose
activities.intendedInsight: Mathematical text, symbols included, should read as grammatical sentences.
activities.rationale: Reading aloud tests the convention that notation is part of the sentence and draws on learners' knowledge of how mathematical expressions are spoken.

difficulties.pattern: Writing a column of equations with arrows or implication symbols and no words.
difficulties.revealedBy: Solutions that reach the correct answer but lose marks for 'insufficient justification' or 'unclear argument'.
difficulties.response: Show the marking criteria and a lecturer's model solution. Treat this as a change of convention, not as a deficiency in mathematical ability.

difficulties.pattern: Confusing 'if' with 'if and only if', or necessary with sufficient conditions, in statements of results.
difficulties.revealedBy: Proofs that establish only one direction of a biconditional, or converse statements presented as equivalent.
difficulties.response: Practise rewording conditionals in several equivalent forms and identifying the converse and contrapositive. Involve the maths lecturer, since this is as much a logic issue as a language one.

difficulties.pattern: Overusing 'obviously' and 'clearly' for steps that are not obvious to the reader.
difficulties.revealedBy: Feedback asking for justification of steps that the writer labelled obvious.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to replace each 'clearly' with the reason it holds. Keep the booster only when the step really is immediate to the intended reader.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a short proof that the square of an even integer is even.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Introduces n with a quantifier, writes n = 2k with k an integer, derives n² = 2(2k²) in a sentence with a justification, and states the conclusion in words.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gets the algebra right but leaves symbols undefined or omits linking words.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives numerical examples instead of a general argument.

guidance.contextNotes: UG mathematics and theoretical computing students meet proofs in early modules, where this support is most valuable; worked solutions with full sentences are a good starting point. At PGT and PGR, emphasise the conventions of mathematical papers (theorem environments, citing results) and typesetting conventions such as those used in LaTeX.
reviewNotes: The EAP research base on mathematical writing is small; recommend collaboration with mathematics staff and analysis of local model solutions.

guidance.summary: Gallie (1956) argued that some concepts, especially evaluative social and political ones, are 'essentially contested': their proper use is permanently disputed. This makes explicit definition and justification an expected move in social science writing. In empirical work, Creswell and Creswell (2018) describe how constructs become variables and measures in quantitative designs, while qualitative research treats concepts as open to participants' meanings. Teaching should help learners show contestation, choose a definition for a reason and carry it consistently through a text.

activities.title: One word, three definitions
learnerActions: Find three definitions of a key concept in your module from different authors or traditions
Tabulate what each includes and excludes and which theoretical position it reflects
Write a paragraph that presents the contestation briefly and adopts one definition with a reason linked to your assignment question
activities.intendedInsight: In the social sciences, defining a concept is an argued choice, not a dictionary look-up.
activities.rationale: Gallie's account of essentially contested concepts explains why markers expect definitions to be positioned and justified.

activities.title: From concept to indicator
learnerActions: Take a concept from your field and propose three indicators or survey items that could measure it
Discuss with a partner what each indicator captures and misses
Write two sentences justifying your indicators and acknowledging one limitation
activities.intendedInsight: Operationalisation narrows a concept, and the narrowing needs to be justified and its limits acknowledged.
activities.rationale: Moving from construct to measure is a standard step in quantitative design, and discussing what is lost develops the critical stance markers value.

difficulties.pattern: Opening with a dictionary definition ('The Oxford Dictionary defines globalisation as…').
difficulties.revealedBy: Introductions that cite general dictionaries for key concepts, with marker comments asking for academic sources.
difficulties.response: Show model introductions that define concepts through the literature, and explain why dictionaries rarely capture disciplinary meanings. Treat dictionary definitions as a starting point for the writer, not for the text.

difficulties.pattern: Shifting between different meanings of a key term across an essay.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays where, for example, 'culture' means nationality in one section and organisational practice in another.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to track every use of the key term in a draft and check it against their stated definition.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a short paragraph defining a contested concept from their field for a specified assignment question.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Shows contestation with sources, adopts a definition for a reason linked to the question and signals how it will be used.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Cites an academic definition but does not acknowledge alternatives or justify the choice.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives a dictionary or common-sense definition.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional social science pathways, introduce contestation and justified definition. UG students meet these demands in essays. At PGT and PGR, operationalisation and conceptual frameworks become central to dissertations and theses.

guidance.summary: Qualitative research depends on texts that readers rarely see: field notes, analytic memos and records of analytic decisions. Emerson et al. (2011) describe field notes as written constructions that combine description with in-process analysis and recommend keeping the two distinguishable. Braun and Clarke (2006) set out phases of thematic analysis and warn against describing themes as simply emerging, and their later account of reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2019) stresses that themes are actively constructed by the researcher, which affects how analysis should be reported. Teaching should treat these process texts as writing that can be practised and connect them to the transparent account of analysis that examiners expect.

activities.title: From memo to meaning
learnerActions: Code a short interview extract in pairs
Write a five-minute analytic memo on one code: what it might mean, how it relates to other codes and what you are unsure about
Exchange memos and identify one interpretation that could become a theme and one alternative reading
activities.intendedInsight: Analytic memos are where interpretation is developed in writing, and they leave a trail that an account of the analysis can draw on.
activities.rationale: Reflexive thematic analysis treats themes as constructed through the researcher’s interpretive work; memo writing makes that work visible and open to revision.

activities.title: Observation versus interpretation in field notes
learnerActions: Watch a short video of a classroom or public setting and write field notes
Highlight words that interpret rather than describe (bored, aggressive, confused)
Rewrite the interpretive phrases as observable description and move interpretations to a separate analytic memo
activities.intendedInsight: Field notes are more useful for analysis when description and interpretation are kept distinguishable.
activities.rationale: Emerson et al. treat field notes as written constructions in which description and analytic commentary have different functions.

difficulties.pattern: Field notes full of judgements such as 'the students were bored'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes that cannot be re-analysed because the observation behind each judgement was not recorded.
difficulties.response: Ask what was seen or heard that led to the judgement, record that, and move the interpretation to a memo. Do not ban interpretation from notes; mark it as such.

difficulties.pattern: Writing that themes 'emerged from the data' and giving no account of how analysis was done.
difficulties.revealedBy: Methods sections with one sentence on analysis and passive constructions that hide analytic decisions.
difficulties.response: Discuss the researcher's active role in analysis and ask learners to describe coding and theme development step by step.

difficulties.pattern: Mixing reflexive thematic analysis with coding-reliability procedures, for example reporting inter-rater agreement in a reflexive design.
difficulties.revealedBy: Accounts of analysis that combine incompatible procedures or terms, and examiners’ questions about coherence.
difficulties.response: Discuss the different assumptions of approaches to thematic analysis and help learners describe the one they used consistently. Treat this as a debated area; supervisors and fields differ.

diagnostic.task: Give a short video or transcript and ask for field notes and a brief analytic memo.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The notes record observable detail with interpretations marked; the memo develops a tentative interpretation tied to specific observations and notes an alternative reading.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The notes mix description and interpretation, or the memo summarises rather than interprets.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The notes are mostly evaluative impressions and the memo shows no analytic development.

guidance.contextNotes: UG students may meet field notes in ethnographic or observational modules and final-year projects. PGT dissertation students in education, the social sciences and health often conduct interviews or observations for the first time and need support with memos and with describing their analysis in the methods chapter. PGR researchers keep extended field and analytic records and must account for their analysis in detail, often in a methodology chapter examined for coherence and reflexivity.
reviewNotes: Findings writing, including the use of participant extracts, belongs to res.qualitative-reporting (R1-29); this topic covers field notes, memos and accounts of analysis.

Approaches to thematic analysis are debated, and fields differ on whether they expect coding-reliability or reflexive approaches; the topic presents reflexive thematic analysis as one widely cited approach, not the only one.

guidance.summary: Policy analysis assignments draw on two broad traditions: problem-solving approaches that appraise options against criteria, and critical approaches such as Bacchi's (2009) 'What's the problem represented to be?', which question how policies construct the problems they address. Both are organised around a problem–response–evaluation structure, which Hoey (1983) describes as a common text pattern. Teaching should clarify which tradition an assignment expects, and should distinguish academic policy analysis from the shorter policy brief written for policy-makers.

activities.title: What is the problem represented to be?
learnerActions: Read a short policy summary and underline how it describes the problem
Discuss what this representation assumes and leaves out, and who it treats as responsible
Write a paragraph comparing the policy's framing with an alternative framing and its implications
activities.intendedInsight: How a problem is framed shapes which solutions seem reasonable, so framing is part of the analysis.
activities.rationale: Bacchi's approach gives learners explicit questions for examining problem representation in policy texts.

activities.title: Options against criteria
learnerActions: Identify two or three policy options for a problem from your field
Agree criteria such as effectiveness, equity, cost and feasibility, and assess each option against them using evidence
Write an evaluation section that leads to a recommendation and acknowledges trade-offs
activities.intendedInsight: Recommendations are credible when they follow from transparent comparison against criteria.
activities.rationale: Building the analysis on the problem–response–evaluation pattern makes the structure of policy argument explicit.

difficulties.pattern: Describing what a policy does and when it was introduced, with little analysis.
difficulties.revealedBy: Assignments dominated by policy history and content, with feedback asking for critical analysis.
difficulties.response: Provide a set of analytical questions (problem framing, evidence, stakeholders, options) and require each section to answer one.

difficulties.pattern: Accepting the policy's own account of the problem as fact.
difficulties.revealedBy: Analyses that adopt government definitions uncritically and evaluate only implementation.
difficulties.response: Practise identifying assumptions in policy texts and comparing framings from different stakeholders.

diagnostic.task: Give a short policy summary and ask the learner to identify how it frames the problem, one stakeholder whose view differs, and one piece of evidence they would need to evaluate it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the framing and its assumptions, a relevant stakeholder perspective and evidence that would test the policy's claims.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies stakeholders and evidence but treats the framing as given.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the policy or gives an unsupported opinion.

guidance.contextNotes: UG social policy, politics and education students meet policy analysis in coursework. PGT programmes in public policy, international development and education often assess it extensively, sometimes alongside policy briefs (grp.policy-brief).
reviewNotes: Overlap with grp.policy-brief: the brief is treated as a short professional genre, this topic as the academic analysis that may underpin it.

guidance.summary: Creswell and Creswell (2018) frame research design as a set of connected choices about philosophical worldview, approach and methods, which gives learners a vocabulary for justification. Move analyses of methods sections (Cotos et al., 2017; Lim, 2006) show that expert writers do more than describe procedures: they justify choices to establish rigour and credibility. Teaching should focus on the language of rationale, the coherence between questions and design, and the honest treatment of trade-offs, and should check with supervisors how much paradigm discussion the field expects.

activities.title: Description or justification?
learnerActions: Read a methodology section from a dissertation in your field
Label each sentence as procedure, justification or limitation
Add justification sentences to a procedure-only paragraph, linking each choice to the research questions
activities.intendedInsight: Methodology writing argues for the design; procedure alone does not show why it is appropriate.
activities.rationale: Move analyses show that justifying procedures is a recognised step in methods sections across disciplines.

activities.title: Paradigm to procedure
learnerActions: Choose a research question in your field
In groups, design two contrasting studies that answer different versions of it from different paradigms
Write a short paragraph explaining what each design can and cannot claim
activities.intendedInsight: Paradigm, design and the type of claim a study can make are linked.
activities.rationale: Creswell and Creswell present design as following from worldview and questions, which contrasting designs make concrete.

difficulties.pattern: Writing a long general account of positivism and interpretivism that is not connected to my study.
difficulties.revealedBy: Methodology chapters with textbook-like paradigm sections and feedback asking 'how does this relate to your study?'.
difficulties.response: Require every paradigm statement to be linked to a decision in the study. Check with supervisors how much paradigm discussion is expected, since it varies by field.

difficulties.pattern: Claiming the chosen method is the best or only way to answer the question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Justifications without acknowledged trade-offs or alternatives.
difficulties.response: Practise language that acknowledges alternatives and limitations while defending the choice.

diagnostic.task: Give a research question and a two-sentence design description and ask the learner to write a justification paragraph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Connects design to question and paradigm, justifies key choices with reasons and acknowledges a trade-off.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Justifies some choices but in general terms, or omits limitations.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the procedure or asserts that the design is appropriate without reasons.

guidance.contextNotes: UG final-year project students need a brief, proportionate justification. PGT dissertation students, often new to social research, need explicit work on paradigm vocabulary and coherence from the start of the programme, building on methods-section writing. PGR researchers write full methodology chapters examined for coherence and reflexivity.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with res.methods, which is treated as the general prerequisite; this topic adds paradigm-level justification typical of social science and education.

guidance.summary: A laboratory or research notebook is a working record written for a future reader: the writer some months later, a supervisor, a collaborator or an auditor. Research-integrity codes such as the European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA, 2023) expect research records to be accurate, preserved and attributable, and the FAIR principles (Wilkinson et al., 2016) frame data and records as things others should be able to find and reuse. Teaching can make explicit the conventions usually picked up by imitation: dating, recording deviations, keeping observation and interpretation distinguishable, correcting without erasing and linking entries to data, samples and code. Rules differ between paper and electronic notebooks and between research groups, so local requirements take precedence.

activities.title: Could someone repeat this?
learnerActions: Exchange a notebook entry from a recent practical or simulated experiment with a partner
Try to reconstruct exactly what was done, noting every point where you would have to guess (quantities, timings, settings, file names)
Revise your own entry so that each gap is filled, and mark any deviation from the planned protocol
activities.intendedInsight: A notebook is judged by whether another competent person could follow and verify the work, not by neatness.
activities.rationale: Testing an entry against a real reader’s needs makes the reproducibility purpose behind integrity guidance concrete, which may make it more memorable than a checklist alone.

activities.title: Observation, calculation, interpretation
learnerActions: Sort sentences from a notebook entry into raw observation, calculation and interpretation
Rewrite an entry in which an interpretation has replaced the observation (for example 'reaction failed') so that what was observed is recorded first
Add links from the entry to the data file, sample label or code version it relates to
activities.intendedInsight: Keeping observation distinct from interpretation, and linking records to data, lets results be re-examined later.
activities.rationale: The FAIR principles stress data that can be found and reused; linking entries to identifiable files and samples is the everyday practice that makes this possible.

difficulties.pattern: I write rough notes during the lab and copy them up neatly afterwards.
difficulties.revealedBy: Tidy notebooks with no corrections, times or deviations, and values that appear to have been rounded or selected after the event.
difficulties.response: Explain that the contemporaneous record, corrections included, is the primary evidence, and that a fair copy can raise questions rather than answer them. Show the group's rule for correcting entries (for example a single line through the error, initialled and dated, or the electronic equivalent). Do not treat neat presentation as the criterion.

difficulties.pattern: Recording only the runs that worked.
difficulties.revealedBy: Failed runs, outliers and changes to the method missing from the record, discovered when results cannot be reproduced.
difficulties.response: Discuss why failed attempts and deviations are informative and how leaving them out can shade into selective reporting. Model brief, neutral entries for unsuccessful runs.

difficulties.pattern: Writing values without units, or abbreviations only I understand.
difficulties.revealedBy: Supervisors or demonstrators unable to interpret entries, and calculation errors traced to unit confusion.
difficulties.response: Use a short self-check for each entry (date, aim, units, identifiers, deviations). Accept symbols and abbreviations that are defined in the notebook. For learners with dyslexia or motor difficulties, an electronic notebook with templates may be a reasonable adjustment.

diagnostic.task: Give a short notebook entry and ask the learner to list what a reader could not verify or repeat from it, and then to rewrite the entry.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the missing date, units, identifiers and an unrecorded deviation, separates observation from interpretation and corrects without erasing the original.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices missing units or date but not the unrecorded deviation, or rewrites the entry as a polished past-tense method section.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Rewrites for neatness or grammar only, without identifying what is missing for reproducibility.

guidance.contextNotes: UG students meet lab books in practical classes, where demonstrators may assess them; focus there on dating, units and recording deviations. PGT research-project students keep the primary record of a short independent project and need the group’s conventions, including electronic notebooks and data-management requirements, from the first week. PGR researchers work under institutional research-integrity and data-management policies, and their records may be consulted in authorship or misconduct questions; linking notebooks to code repositories and data management plans matters here. Computational researchers may keep records in notebooks such as Jupyter or in version-control histories, and fieldwork records follow the same principles.
reviewNotes: There is little EAP research on laboratory notebooks; the guidance draws on research-integrity and data-management guidance and should be checked against departmental rules.
Notebook rules for regulated or industry-linked research (for example good laboratory practice or records kept for patent purposes) are stricter and are not covered in detail.

guidance.summary: Clinical reasoning writing asks students to show thinking that practitioners often do quickly and tacitly. Levett-Jones et al. (2010) describe a clinical reasoning cycle (considering the situation, collecting and processing cues, identifying problems, establishing goals, taking action, evaluating outcomes and reflecting) that many nursing programmes use as an assignment scaffold, and evidence-based practice (Sackett et al., 1996) supplies the expectation that interventions are justified by evidence, expertise and patient preference. The language work lies in turning these steps into connected argument: naming cues, inferring cautiously, prioritising explicitly and justifying with citation. Programmes use different models, so the programme’s own framework and exemplars should be used.

activities.title: Cue, inference, priority
learnerActions: Read a short patient scenario and underline the cues (observations, history, what the patient says)
For each cue, write one sentence stating what it may indicate, using hedged language
Rank the problems you have identified and write a sentence justifying the top priority
activities.intendedInsight: Visible reasoning links each judgement to specific evidence in the case and gives an explicit reason for priority.
activities.rationale: The clinical reasoning cycle treats collecting and processing cues and identifying problems as distinct steps; separating them in writing is intended to make the reasoning assessable.

activities.title: Why this intervention?
learnerActions: Take a list of interventions for a scenario that has no rationales
Add to each a because-clause linking it to the assessment and a citation to evidence or a guideline
Review a partner's rationales by asking what in the patient's data makes each intervention appropriate
activities.intendedInsight: An intervention is justified by its link to this patient's assessment as well as by evidence in general.
activities.rationale: Evidence-based practice integrates research evidence with clinical expertise and patient circumstances, so a rationale that cites only research is incomplete.

difficulties.pattern: Describing what I would do, step by step, without saying why.
difficulties.revealedBy: Assignments that list actions in sequence, with feedback such as 'rationale?' or 'link to the evidence'.
difficulties.response: Require a because-clause or citation for each action and show an exemplar paragraph annotated for its reasoning moves. Do not respond by asking for more actions; ask for fewer, better-justified ones.

difficulties.pattern: Stating a diagnosis or problem with certainty from limited data.
difficulties.revealedBy: Claims such as 'the patient has sepsis' based on a single observation, and markers' comments on unsupported conclusions.
difficulties.response: Teach the distinction between a cue, an inference and a confirmed finding, and practise hedged and conditional formulations. Some programmes reserve diagnostic language for particular professions, so use 'problem' or 'need' where the programme expects it.

difficulties.pattern: My placement does things differently from the textbook, so I am not sure which to write about.
difficulties.revealedBy: Assignments that hide observed practice or present it uncritically, and learners asking which version is 'right'.
difficulties.response: Explain that assignments usually expect evidence-based practice while allowing observed practice to be discussed professionally and anonymously. Module leaders should state how placement observations may be used in assessed writing, since briefs often leave this unclear.

diagnostic.task: Give a brief scenario and ask the learner to explain in one paragraph which problem is the priority and why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Cites specific cues, hedges inferences, gives an explicit criterion for priority (such as risk of deterioration) and links to a guideline or evidence.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies a reasonable priority but justifies it generally ('this is the most important') or without reference to the scenario.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the patient or lists actions without identifying or justifying a priority.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional pathways for health master’s entrants, many of them experienced practitioners, introduce the idea that tacit clinical judgement must be made explicit and referenced. In UG nursing, midwifery, pharmacy and allied-health programmes, clinical reasoning is assessed from the first year in scenario-based essays, care plans and practical-examination rationales; embed work in those assignments with clinical educators. At PGT, advanced-practice and pre-registration master’s students write more complex case analyses in which reasoning must engage with guidelines, service context and conflicting evidence. Terminology differs between professions and countries (nursing diagnosis, clinical impression, problem list), so follow the programme’s language.
reviewNotes: The clinical reasoning cycle is one of several models used in health education; the topic is model-neutral and cites the cycle as a common scaffold, not a requirement.
Pharmacy and medicine document reasoning in different forms (for example pharmaceutical care plans or problem lists); exemplars should come from the learner’s profession.

guidance.summary: Care plans are structured documents whose logic runs from assessment to evaluation: each problem should be traceable to assessment data, each goal to a problem, each intervention to a goal and each evaluation criterion back to its goal. The nursing process supplies this structure, and programmes add a nursing model or documentation standard on top of it, so EAP teaching should start from the programme’s template. Nesi and Gardner (2012) show that case-based health assignments apply professional knowledge to a specific case, and care-planning assignments add an evidence-based rationale for each intervention in the sense of evidence-based practice (Sackett et al., 1996). Much of the language work lies in goal-writing and rationales, where students often write tasks rather than outcomes.

activities.title: Tasks or outcomes?
learnerActions: Sort goal statements into practitioner tasks (for example 'monitor fluid intake') and patient outcomes (for example 'the patient will drink at least 1.5 litres a day by Friday')
Rewrite each task as a measurable, time-bound patient outcome
Check each rewritten goal against the problem it addresses and the evaluation criterion that will measure it
activities.intendedInsight: Goals describe what will change for the patient, and must be measurable so that evaluation is possible.
activities.rationale: Goal-writing is where the logic of a plan most often breaks; making the outcome orientation explicit connects each goal to its evaluation and to the case-study purpose of applying knowledge to a particular patient.

activities.title: Linking need to intervention
learnerActions: Read a care plan with goals and interventions but no rationales
Add an evidence-based rationale for each intervention, citing a source or guideline
Write an evaluation criterion for each goal and check that it measures the goal as worded
activities.intendedInsight: A care plan is an argument from assessed need to intervention to evaluation, and every link needs justification.
activities.rationale: Making rationales explicit connects care planning to evidence-based practice, in which interventions are justified by evidence, expertise and the patient’s circumstances.

difficulties.pattern: Writing goals as things the nurse will do.
difficulties.revealedBy: Goals such as 'to monitor blood pressure', and evaluation sections that report actions taken rather than outcomes achieved.
difficulties.response: Use the tasks-or-outcomes activity and a sentence frame for patient-centred goals. Do not simply give a SMART acronym; check that each goal can actually be evaluated.

difficulties.pattern: Using a care-plan format or abbreviations from a previous hospital, country or textbook.
difficulties.revealedBy: Templates, headings or abbreviations that do not match the programme's model or the local approved list.
difficulties.response: Treat the programme's model and approved-abbreviation list as the reference, and discuss differences from learners' previous practice as professional variation, not error.

difficulties.pattern: Labelling the patient by their condition or behaviour ('the diabetic', 'non-compliant').
difficulties.revealedBy: Feedback on language that is not person-centred, often in otherwise sound plans.
difficulties.response: Teach person-centred alternatives and the reasons for them, following the programme's guidance, and note that preferred terms differ between communities and change over time.

diagnostic.task: Give an assessment summary and a care-plan row with a weak goal and no rationale, and ask the learner to improve it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Rewrites the goal as a measurable patient outcome with a timescale, adds an evidenced rationale and an evaluation criterion that matches the goal.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Improves the goal but leaves the rationale generic, or writes an evaluation that does not measure the goal.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Changes wording only, leaving a task-based goal and no rationale.

guidance.contextNotes: UG nursing students write care plans from the first year, often within case-study assignments and alongside placement documentation; embed support with clinical educators and the programme’s template. On pre-registration master’s programmes and some advanced-practice modules, care planning is assessed with more emphasis on evidence, risk and interprofessional context. Documentation standards and nursing models differ between countries and institutions, so learners who trained elsewhere may bring a different but valid model.
reviewNotes: Nursing models (for example activities-of-living models) and documentation standards vary by programme and country; no specific model is cited, and teachers should use the programme’s own.
Care plans in clinical records follow legal and organisational documentation rules that differ from those of academic care-planning assignments.

guidance.summary: Accounting and finance students write about numbers for readers who will act on them: investors, managers, auditors or lenders. Zhu (2004) found that business-course assignments often simulate professional genres written for business readers, and the commentary genres of finance follow the general pattern of data commentary while adding evaluation of performance and hedged projection. Corporate narratives are a reading as well as a writing challenge: research on impression management (Merkl-Davies & Brennan, 2007) shows that narrative disclosures can present results selectively and favourably, so students need to test evaluative claims against the figures. Appraisal theory (Martin & White, 2005) gives teachers tools for showing how evaluation is built into apparently neutral financial prose.

activities.title: From figures to judgement
learnerActions: Read a table of two years’ results and write three sentences that only describe changes
Add a sentence to each that explains a likely driver, hedged appropriately
Add a final sentence evaluating what the results mean for a named reader, such as a lender or shareholder
activities.intendedInsight: Financial commentary moves from accurate description to explanation and evaluation for a particular user.
activities.rationale: Commentary that only restates figures is a frequent criticism; building the explanation and evaluation layers separately makes the expected moves visible and keeps the professional reader in view.

activities.title: Testing the narrative
learnerActions: Highlight the evaluative words in a chair's or chief executive's statement (for example strong, resilient, challenging)
Check each evaluative claim against the financial statements and note whether the figures support it
Rewrite one paragraph as a neutral analyst's commentary
activities.intendedInsight: Corporate narratives evaluate as well as inform, and an analyst's commentary tests those evaluations against evidence.
activities.rationale: Research on impression management in corporate narratives, and appraisal analysis of evaluative language, both suggest that critical reading of disclosure language is a distinct skill worth teaching.

difficulties.pattern: Listing every figure and change without saying which ones matter.
difficulties.revealedBy: Commentaries that restate tables line by line, with feedback asking for analysis.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to choose the three most significant changes for the named reader and to justify the choice. Do not simply ask for more ratios.

difficulties.pattern: Confusing percentage and percentage-point change, or stating forecasts as facts.
difficulties.revealedBy: Numerical errors in commentary and unhedged statements such as 'the share price will rise'.
difficulties.response: Use short accuracy drills with real figures and a checklist of the assumptions behind every forecast.
