difficulties.pattern: The terms I learned in my previous accounting course are different here.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mixed terminology (for example turnover and revenue, stock and inventory) and uncertainty about which reporting framework a module assumes.
difficulties.response: Treat terminology from other frameworks and varieties as a resource and build a comparison glossary. Module teams should state which reporting framework and terminology an assignment assumes, since briefs often leave this implicit.

diagnostic.task: Give a small table of results and ask for a three-sentence commentary for a shareholder.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Selects the most significant change, reports it accurately, explains a plausible driver with a hedge and evaluates the implication for the shareholder.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reports changes accurately but only describes them, or evaluates without supporting figures.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates figures without selection, or makes errors in calculating or describing changes.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional pathways for finance and accounting master’s programmes, introduce the commentary pattern and accurate number language using real annual reports. UG accounting and finance students meet these genres in financial reporting, analysis and audit modules alongside numerical examinations. On MSc Finance and Accounting programmes, which recruit large international cohorts, commentary, valuation reports and analyses of disclosures are central to coursework and dissertations, and some students already hold professional qualifications whose terminology differs from the module’s.
reviewNotes: Reporting frameworks (for example IFRS and national standards) and terminology differ between jurisdictions; teachers should confirm which the programme uses.
The EAP research base on student accounting and finance writing is small; the guidance draws on business-writing and corporate-disclosure research and should be checked against local exemplars.

guidance.summary: Consultancy projects, live or simulated, are now common capstones on business master’s programmes and some UG degrees, and they combine a professional report genre with academic assessment. Nathan (2013) shows that the business case report is problem- and decision-oriented, and the consultancy report extends this to a real reader whose priorities, vocabulary and time shape the text. Bhatia’s (1993) analysis of professional genres supports teaching the report through its communicative purpose and readers, and Zhu (2004) shows that business-course assignments draw on professional as well as academic conventions. The main teaching challenge is the dual readership: what persuades a client and what earns marks are related but not identical.

activities.title: Two readers, one recommendation
learnerActions: Take one recommendation from a project and write it twice: once for the client's managing director and once for the module marker
Compare length, order, terminology and the role of theory and citation in the two versions
Agree as a team where each version belongs in the submission
activities.intendedInsight: The client wants actionable advice; the marker wants to see how analysis and theory support it.
activities.rationale: Contrasting the same content for two readers makes the genre’s dual purpose explicit, in line with genre analysis that starts from communicative purpose.

activities.title: Making recommendations actionable
learnerActions: Review the recommendations in a past or draft report
Add who, what, when, cost and risk to each recommendation
Rank the recommendations by impact and feasibility and justify the order in one sentence each
activities.intendedInsight: Recommendations are judged on feasibility and priority as well as on their link to evidence.
activities.rationale: Business case reports are judged on recommendations that follow from the analysis and can be implemented; adding implementation detail tests both.

difficulties.pattern: Writing the client report like an academic essay, with theory first and recommendations at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Client feedback that the report is hard to use, and long literature sections in client-facing text.
difficulties.response: Show model client reports and the module's guidance on where theory belongs. Do not tell learners to remove theory altogether; it often belongs in a separate academic section or appendix.

difficulties.pattern: Accepting everything the client asks for, or never questioning the brief.
difficulties.revealedBy: Scope creep, unclear objectives and reports that do not answer the agreed question.
difficulties.response: Practise scoping meetings and written confirmation of the brief, including polite language for negotiating scope. Supervisors should model how to renegotiate a brief, since students often lack authority with real clients.

difficulties.pattern: Some team members' contributions disappear from the final report.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uneven sections, complaints about workload and reflective accounts that describe conflict.
difficulties.response: Agree roles and drafting and editing processes early, and give everyone a visible section or task. Module teams should design peer assessment and contribution statements that do not penalise quieter members or those writing in an additional language.

diagnostic.task: Give a client brief and one paragraph of findings, and ask for a three-sentence recommendation for the client.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Leads with a specific, feasible action, links it to the findings and gives responsibility, timescale or cost in plain language.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Links the recommendation to the findings but is vague about implementation, or uses an academic register and citations unsuited to the client.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the findings or gives a generic recommendation not grounded in them.

guidance.contextNotes: In UG business programmes, consultancy-style projects usually appear in the final year, often in teams with simulated clients. On PGT programmes such as MSc Management and the MBA, live consultancy projects often replace or sit alongside the dissertation, so support should begin with scoping the brief and continue through the report and the reflective account. Requirements for confidentiality, client sign-off and the balance between client report and academic reflection differ between schools, so the module handbook is the reference.
reviewNotes: No EAP study of student consultancy reports is in the bibliography; the guidance extends research on business case reports and professional genres and should be checked with module leaders.

guidance.summary: A moot is a simulated appellate hearing in which students argue a point of law before a judge, usually in pairs against an opposing team. It combines written preparation (the skeleton argument and bundle of authorities) with oral delivery and live interaction, and judges commonly assess the ability to respond to questions from the bench. Twining and Miers (2010) treat legal argument as the interpretation of rules and their application to facts, which supplies the content of each ground, while Joughin (1998) shows that oral assessments differ in how interactive they are and in what they reward, which helps teachers and students see what is being judged. Teaching should rehearse interventions, not only prepared speeches.

activities.title: Interrupt me, please
learnerActions: Prepare a two-minute submission on one ground with two authorities
Deliver it while a peer acting as judge interrupts with prepared questions
After each answer, practise a bridging phrase that returns to your submission, then discuss which answers were direct
activities.intendedInsight: Responding to the bench is part of the argument, not an interruption of it.
activities.rationale: Interactive oral assessment rewards responsiveness; rehearsing interruptions is intended to prepare learners for a feature that a prepared script does not address.

activities.title: From written answer to skeleton argument
learnerActions: Take a written answer to a problem question and reduce one issue to a skeleton argument of grounds and authorities
Compare it with a model skeleton argument for length and structure
Practise citing each authority aloud in the spoken form expected in court
activities.intendedInsight: Oral argument is built from the same legal analysis as written work but is selected, ordered and cited differently.
activities.rationale: Building the skeleton from a written answer makes the dependence on problem-question analysis, and on applying rules to facts, explicit.

difficulties.pattern: Reading a prepared script and losing my place when the judge asks a question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fluent delivery that breaks down at interventions, and little contact with the bench.
difficulties.response: Rehearse with frequent interruptions using short notes rather than full scripts, and normalise asking the judge to repeat a question. Assessors should be clear about how interventions are marked; learners who stammer, are autistic or experience anxiety may need agreed adjustments to format or timing.

difficulties.pattern: Reading out full written citations, or using conversational forms of address.
difficulties.revealedBy: Submissions slowed by citations read in full, and judges' comments on register.
difficulties.response: Model the spoken form of citation and the forms of address for the relevant court, and practise them as fixed expressions.

difficulties.pattern: Refusing to concede anything, because conceding feels like losing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Persisting with an untenable point under questioning and losing credibility and time.
difficulties.response: Show how strategic concession and distinguishing protect the stronger grounds, using model recordings or transcripts.

diagnostic.task: Ask a question from the bench during a short prepared submission.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Answers directly, cites or distinguishes an authority if relevant, and returns to the submission with a signposting phrase.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Answers, but at length or indirectly, or does not return to the structure of the submission.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Ignores or misunderstands the question, or carries on reading from the script.

guidance.contextNotes: On LLB programmes, mooting is usually introduced in the first or second year, sometimes as an assessed part of legal skills modules and sometimes as an extracurricular competition; support should focus on skeleton arguments, oral citation and interventions. LLM students may meet moots in international or commercial law modules and competitions, and those trained in systems with less adversarial oral procedure may find the format unfamiliar. Forms of address and citation differ between jurisdictions and courts, so follow the moot rules provided.
reviewNotes: No applied linguistic study of mooting is in the bibliography; the guidance is based on legal-skills practice and general research on oral assessment and should be reviewed with law staff.
Conventions here follow the appellate model of England and Wales; other jurisdictions and international moot competitions have their own rules.

guidance.summary: Law dissertations are a particular challenge for writers trained on general research-writing models, because doctrinal legal research analyses authoritative texts to establish, explain and critique the law rather than reporting empirical data. Hutchinson and Duncan (2012) describe doctrinal research as a method with its own rigour that is often left implicit, while socio-legal, comparative and theoretical approaches import methods from other disciplines and need their own justification. Paltridge and Starfield (2020) show that thesis structures vary and that students benefit from analysing theses in their own field. EAP support should help students state their method explicitly, design chapters around an argument and manage authority and referencing over a long text.

activities.title: From topic to legal problem
learnerActions: Write your dissertation topic as a phrase (for example, liability for autonomous vehicles)
Rewrite it as a question that identifies a gap, conflict or uncertainty in the law
Identify the method the question calls for and write two sentences justifying it
activities.intendedInsight: A legal research question names a problem in the law, and the method follows from the kind of problem.
activities.rationale: Doctrinal method is often left implicit; making the question and the method explicit responds to the expectation, set out by Hutchinson and Duncan, that legal researchers can describe what they do.

activities.title: Chapter functions
learnerActions: Analyse the contents pages and chapter introductions of two law theses or LLM dissertations
Label each chapter by its function in the argument (establishing the law, critique, comparison, proposal)
Draft your own chapter plan with a one-sentence function statement for each chapter
activities.intendedInsight: Each chapter of a legal dissertation should advance the argument, not survey an area.
activities.rationale: Analysing local exemplars of thesis structure helps writers see how general macrostructures are adapted in law.

difficulties.pattern: Writing chapters that describe the law in an area without a question driving them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Supervisor feedback such as 'too descriptive' or 'what is your argument?', and conclusions that summarise rather than answer.
difficulties.response: Require a chapter-level claim and a link back to the research question at the start and end of each chapter. Do not ask for more coverage; ask for selection.

difficulties.pattern: Copying an empirical methodology chapter from another discipline, or leaving out method because doctrinal research 'has no method'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Methodology sections that discuss sampling and data collection irrelevant to doctrinal work, or no account of method at all.
difficulties.response: Show how doctrinal and socio-legal dissertations state their methods, and agree with supervisors what is expected locally.

difficulties.pattern: Losing control of footnotes and authorities across a long text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent citation forms, missing pinpoints and tables of authorities that do not match the text.
difficulties.response: Introduce reference-management and checking routines early; formatting is a late-stage task, but time for it should be scheduled.

diagnostic.task: Ask for a one-paragraph statement of the dissertation’s research question and method.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States a legal problem, names the method with a reason and indicates the expected contribution.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a topic or question but leaves the method implicit or unjustified.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes an area of law without a question or method.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional programmes for LLM entrants, introduce legal method and research questions through short proposals. LLB students who choose a dissertation option need early help with question design. LLM dissertations are short and written under time pressure, so support focuses on the question, the method statement and the chapter plan. Doctoral law researchers write theses on a different scale, often combining doctrinal and socio-legal work, and need support with sustained argument, contribution and publication. Expectations about method chapters differ between law schools and jurisdictions.
reviewNotes: Legal research methods are debated, including the status of doctrinal research as a method; the topic presents the main approaches without ranking them.
The topic assumes common-law legal research; comparative and civil-law dissertations may follow other structures.

guidance.summary: The psychology report is a closely conventionalised genre: the APA Publication Manual (American Psychological Association, 2020) specifies its structure, statistical reporting and bias-free language, and departments usually add their own guide. Beyond format, the genre carries the discipline’s view of evidence: hypotheses are derived from theory, results are reported so that effect sizes and uncertainty are visible, and conclusions are calibrated to the data. Cumming (2014) argues for estimation with effect sizes and confidence intervals, and the ASA statement on p-values (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016) sets out common misinterpretations of significance testing; markers increasingly expect students to interpret results in these terms. Teaching is likely to be most useful when it draws on departmental exemplars and the module’s own statistics output.

activities.title: From output to sentence
learnerActions: Take a statistics output table from a practical class
Identify the values that must be reported (test statistic, degrees of freedom, p, effect size, confidence interval)
Write the results sentence in APA format, then add a plain-language sentence saying what the result means for the hypothesis
activities.intendedInsight: A results sentence turns software output into a conventional, interpretable claim.
activities.rationale: Reporting effect sizes and intervals, not only p values, reflects the estimation approach Cumming recommends.

activities.title: From hypothesis to discussion
learnerActions: Highlight each hypothesis in an exemplar introduction
Find where each hypothesis is tested in the results and discussed in the discussion
Draft a discussion paragraph for a non-significant result that does not claim the hypothesis was disproved
activities.intendedInsight: The report is organised around its hypotheses, and each must be followed through to the discussion.
activities.rationale: Tracing hypotheses through an exemplar makes the genre’s logic visible, and the non-significant case addresses misreadings of p values that the ASA statement warns against.

difficulties.pattern: Copying p = .000 from the software output, or reporting only whether a result was significant.
difficulties.revealedBy: Results without effect sizes, or with impossible exact p values.
difficulties.response: Teach the convention explicitly (p < .001) and show why effect sizes and intervals are expected. Avoid treating this as carelessness; it follows from how software displays output.

difficulties.pattern: A non-significant result means there is no effect, so my study failed.
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussions claiming that the null hypothesis was proved, or apologetic discussions of 'failed' studies.
difficulties.response: Discuss what non-significance does and does not show, including statistical power and confidence intervals, and model neutral discussion language.

difficulties.pattern: Writing the introduction as a general literature review that does not lead to the hypotheses.
difficulties.revealedBy: Hypotheses that appear without a rationale, and markers' comments on the structure of the introduction.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to write the hypotheses first and then check that each paragraph of the introduction contributes to the rationale for one of them.

diagnostic.task: Give a statistics output and a hypothesis, and ask for a results sentence and a one-sentence interpretation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Reports the statistic, degrees of freedom, p, effect size and interval in APA format and relates the result to the hypothesis with calibrated language.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Formats the statistic correctly but omits the effect size, or misstates the relation to the hypothesis.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Reports only significant or non-significant, or copies output values without interpretation.

guidance.contextNotes: UG psychology students write reports from the first year, and in accredited programmes the empirical project is a substantial final-year requirement; embed support in research-methods modules. Conversion master’s students may come from other disciplines and need a rapid induction into the genre and its statistics. Preregistration and other open-research practices increasingly shape method and results sections at PGT level and beyond (see pub.open-research). Qualitative psychology reports follow different conventions, partly covered by res.qualitative-reporting.
reviewNotes: Departmental conventions vary (for example on stating hypotheses and on report length); the department’s guide takes precedence over general APA advice.
The topic follows the 7th edition of the APA Publication Manual; APA style is revised periodically.

guidance.summary: Education and TESOL practice genres sit between professional documents and academic writing: a lesson plan is a working document, but its rationale is an academic argument, and a teaching-practice reflection is assessed for analysis, not narration. Schön’s (1983) reflective practitioner and Moon’s (2004) account of reflective learning underpin much teacher-education assessment, while classroom research reports adapt general research design (Creswell & Creswell, 2018) to practitioner enquiry. Many MA TESOL students are experienced teachers whose expertise is a resource; the writing challenge is to connect it explicitly to literature and evidence. Programme templates and exemplars are essential, as genres and criteria differ widely.

activities.title: Why this stage?
learnerActions: Read a lesson plan and annotate each stage with the questions 'why here?' and 'why this?'
Write a rationale sentence for each stage that refers to the learners and to a principle or study
Compare rationales with a partner and identify any that rely only on personal preference
activities.intendedInsight: A lesson-plan rationale is an argument that justifies decisions by the learners’ needs and by theory.
activities.rationale: Making the reasoning behind planning explicit reflects the reflective-practitioner view that professional knowledge can be articulated and examined.

activities.title: From description to analysis in teaching-practice reflection
learnerActions: Read two reflections on the same observed lesson, one mainly descriptive and one analytic
Identify the sentences that link classroom evidence to principles and propose changes
Rewrite a descriptive paragraph from your own reflection using that pattern
activities.intendedInsight: Teaching-practice reflections are assessed on analysis and action, not on the account of what happened.
activities.rationale: Moon distinguishes descriptive writing from deeper reflection; comparing the two side by side makes the expected depth visible.

difficulties.pattern: My teaching experience is evidence enough, so I do not need to cite literature.
difficulties.revealedBy: Rationales and reflections built on anecdote, with feedback asking for engagement with the literature.
difficulties.response: Value experience explicitly and show how to pair each experiential claim with a source that supports, qualifies or challenges it. Do not imply that experienced teachers’ knowledge is invalid.

difficulties.pattern: Evaluating materials by whether I liked them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Materials evaluations without criteria, or with criteria that are not justified.
difficulties.response: Build or adopt a set of criteria with learners and require each judgement to cite a criterion and evidence from the materials.

difficulties.pattern: Generalising from one class to all learners of a nationality or level ('learners from my country prefer…').
difficulties.revealedBy: Classroom research reports that make claims about whole groups from a single class.
difficulties.response: Practise scoping claims to the context and discuss what practitioner research can and cannot claim. Address essentialising language explicitly and respectfully.

diagnostic.task: Give one stage of a short lesson plan and ask for a two-sentence rationale.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Justifies the stage by the learners’ needs and a named principle or study, and anticipates a likely issue.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a plausible reason but without reference to the learners or the literature.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes what happens in the stage rather than why.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional programmes for education and TESOL master’s entrants, introduce the rationale and reflective genres through short tasks that build on participants’ teaching experience. UG education and initial teacher-education students write lesson plans and placement reflections assessed against professional standards. On MA TESOL and education master’s programmes, which recruit large international cohorts, materials evaluation, teaching-practice reflection and small-scale classroom research are central; many students are experienced teachers new to writing about their practice academically. Teacher-education conventions and professional standards differ between countries.
reviewNotes: The bibliography has no specific study of TESOL practice genres; the guidance draws on reflective-practice and research-design sources and should be checked with programme staff.
Some MA TESOL programmes have no teaching-practice component; choose genres to match the programme.

guidance.summary: The exegesis is a research genre in which the writer is also the maker of the work being examined. Hamilton and Jaaniste (2010) found that practice-led exegeses commonly combine situating concepts, precedents of practice and a researcher-centred account of the practice, and they propose a connective model in which the text links the practice to its field. Schön’s (1983) account of reflection-in-action offers a way to describe making as inquiry, and Paltridge and Starfield (2020) show that thesis types and structures vary across fields, which applies strongly here. Because the balance between practice and text, the name of the text (exegesis, critical commentary, contextual report) and the expected voice differ between institutions, teaching should start from the learner’s own regulations and examples.

activities.title: Mapping an exegesis
learnerActions: Read the contents pages and introductions of two exegeses or practice-based theses from your institution
Label each section as context, precedents, methodology, account of practice or contribution
Draft a contents plan for your own exegesis and note how each section connects to the work
activities.intendedInsight: An exegesis connects the practice to its field, and each section has a function in that connection.
activities.rationale: Hamilton and Jaaniste’s analysis of exegesis structures provides categories that make the components of the genre visible.

activities.title: Making as method
learnerActions: Choose three images from your process documentation that show turning points
For each, write a paragraph explaining what you were testing, what you noticed and what changed as a result
Revise the paragraphs to link each turning point to your research question
activities.intendedInsight: Process documentation becomes research writing when decisions are explained as moves in an inquiry.
activities.rationale: Schön’s reflection-in-action describes how practitioners learn through making; articulating it links the practice to the research question.

difficulties.pattern: Writing a description of my work and biography instead of an argument.
difficulties.revealedBy: Exegeses organised as a chronological account of making, with feedback asking for the research question and contribution.
difficulties.response: Ask for a one-sentence statement of question and contribution and test each section against it. Do not ask learners to give up a personal voice; first-person accounts of practice are usually expected.

difficulties.pattern: Using theory as decoration, quoting theorists without connecting them to the work.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long theoretical sections followed by accounts of practice that do not refer back to them.
difficulties.response: Require each theoretical source to be linked to a specific decision or feature of the work. Present the role of theory as debated in the field, not as a fixed requirement.

difficulties.pattern: The regulations and my supervisors give different messages about what the text should do.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uncertainty about length, voice, the status of documentation and how examiners will weigh text against practice.
difficulties.response: Help learners compare the regulations with recent successful examples and prepare questions for supervisors. Institutions should state assessment criteria for practice and text explicitly, since the genre is contested.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a 100-word paragraph stating what their practice investigates and what it contributes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States a question or concern, situates it in a field or practice and makes a hedged claim about contribution.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a concern and context but no contribution, or claims a contribution without context.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the work or the maker’s background only.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional programmes for art and design master’s entrants, introduce writing about one’s practice as research through short contextualising texts. On MA and MFA programmes, a critical or contextual report often accompanies the final project, so support focuses on contextualisation and the link between text and work. Doctoral researchers in practice-based or practice-led programmes write a full exegesis examined alongside the practice and need sustained support with method, contribution and their institution’s regulations, which vary widely between countries.
reviewNotes: The relationship between practice and text in practice-based doctorates is contested (for example whether the text explains, frames or is itself part of the research); the topic does not take a side.
Terminology (exegesis, critical commentary, contextual report, thesis) and weighting rules vary; the institution’s regulations take precedence.

authorNotes: Architecture, music, film and media, and performing arts have no specific topics beyond dad.practice-research-exegesis; music (programme notes, analysis) and film or media (shot analysis, production documentation) remain notable gaps.
dad.design-rationale overlaps with grp.technical-design-report and dse.protocols-specifications; the boundary is drawn here between visual, reflective design rationale and engineering documentation.
Contextual or critical studies essays in art and design are not represented except through dad.visual-analysis and dhu.interpretive-argument.

dbe.business-case-analysis overlaps with grp.case-study, dbe.professional-genres and dbe.consultancy-report overlap with grp.business-report and grp.executive-summary. The DBE topics are framed as business-school realisations of those general genres.
Economics has only one topic (dbe.economic-reasoning); empirical economics writing (reporting regressions, policy evaluation) is not covered beyond res.quantitative-reporting.

Health genres still missing: clinical documentation and record-keeping, OSCE communication (only exm.exam-formats mentions OSCEs) and structured handover beyond dhl.professional-communication. Care plans and case presentations are now separate topics, and clinical reasoning has its own topic.
dhl.reflective-practice could be generalised to other professional programmes (social work); education reflection is now covered within dss.education-practice-genres.
History has no topic on historiography or historical explanation as such; it is partly covered under dhu.interpretive-argument and dhu.primary-sources.
Languages, linguistics, translation studies and area studies have no specific topics, although they recruit many multilingual students.
dhu.close-reading leans towards literary studies; close reading of visual texts is in dad.visual-analysis.
Legal research skills (Westlaw, Lexis, finding and updating authorities) are covered only generically by inf.databases, linked from dlw.legal-research-writing.
The DLW topics assume common-law (primarily English) legal English; contexts teaching EU, international or comparative law have different text types.
DSE is broad: it covers natural sciences, engineering, mathematics and computing with seven topics. Missing genres include code review and commit messages and statistics write-ups for data science.
dse.scientific-language overlaps with grm.nominalisation and reg.disciplinary-style; it is framed as the functional, Hallidayan view of scientific register built on those topics.
dse.software-documentation bundles four genres (README, comments, API reference, design documents) with different readers; it could be split if computing coverage is expanded.
dse.lab-notebooks could usefully become a prerequisite of grp.lab-report and of res.methods in their groups’ files.

dss.methodology-justification overlaps with res.methods, which is its general prerequisite; dss.qualitative-writing now covers process texts only, leaving findings to res.qualitative-reporting (which could take dss.qualitative-writing as a soft prerequisite).

Stage roles: ESAP topics are core mainly at in-sessional-ug or in-sessional-pgt for their disciplines, with foundation core limited to dse.scientific-language, dse.scientific-explanation and dad.visual-analysis. dse.mathematical-writing, dse.protocols-specifications, dhl.evidence-based-practice and the DBE topics no longer carry foundation (R1-08, R3-17); dlw.legal-language, dhu.close-reading and three DAD topics keep foundation with cefrStart lowered to B1+.
